title: Misen (Taiwan Ramen Originator)
summary: The Imaike neighborhood Chinese restaurant where a Taiwanese immigrant chef invented 'Taiwan ramen,' a fiery noodle dish that, confusingly, doesn't actually exist in Taiwan.
description:
Despite the name, Taiwan ramen was invented in Nagoya, not Taiwan: a chef originally from Taiwan running this restaurant in the Imaike neighborhood adapted a spicy Taiwanese noodle dish for local tastes decades ago, and the result, topped with minced pork, chili, and garlic in a fiery broth, became popular enough to spread across the city under a name that still confuses first-time visitors. Misen is generally credited as the restaurant where the dish originated, making it a genuine culinary landmark rather than just another ramen shop.

A bowl is priced like a typical noodle-shop meal, and the heat level can be intense, so it's worth asking about spice options if you're not used to Sichuan-style chili oil. A meal takes about thirty minutes.

The restaurant sits in a fairly local, unassuming stretch of Imaike rather than a tourist zone, so it rarely feels overrun, though a lunch or dinner rush from neighborhood regulars is common at peak hours; timing a visit slightly off those peaks makes for an easier, unhurried meal.
access: Short walk from Imaike Station (Higashiyama or Tsurumai subway line)

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Nagoya regional noodle food tour

title: Shinsakaemachi Shopping Arcade
summary: A slightly worn, Showa-era shopping arcade near Sakae stacked with idol goods shops, secondhand record stores, and hobby shops that draw subculture fans rather than casual tourists.
description:
Just off the polished main streets of Sakae, this covered arcade and its surrounding underground passages retain a distinctly older, rougher-edged atmosphere, with narrow storefronts given over to idol merchandise, trading cards, secondhand records, retro video games, and various niche hobby goods. It's the kind of place that rewards actually going shop to shop rather than expecting a curated experience, since the appeal is in the density and unpredictability of what's stocked.

Browsing costs nothing, and how much time it takes depends entirely on how deep an interest you have in the specific subcultures represented; an hour covers a reasonable loop for a casual visitor.

It draws a knowledgeable but low-key crowd of hobbyists rather than crowds of tourists, and most shops stay comfortably navigable even on weekends. Because some of the storefronts and passages feel a little worn and dimly lit compared with mainstream Sakae, it's easy to walk past the entrance without realizing what's inside — worth deliberately seeking out rather than stumbling upon.
access: Short walk from Sakae Station (Higashiyama and Meijo subway lines)

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Nagoya subculture and pop-culture tour

title: Sunshine Sakae Ferris Wheel
summary: A small rooftop Ferris wheel perched atop a Sakae shopping complex, offering a compact night view over the neon of downtown Nagoya.
description:
Rising from the roof of a shopping and entertainment complex in the middle of Sakae, this Ferris wheel is modest in scale compared with dedicated theme-park attractions, but that's part of its charm — a quick, inexpensive ride that puts you above the neon signage and traffic of downtown for a few minutes without requiring a special trip out of the city center. The complex below houses shops, an arcade, and dining options if you want to extend the stop.

A single ride is inexpensive and takes only a few minutes, making it an easy add-on rather than a planned centerpiece of a visit.

Evenings are clearly the best time to ride, when the surrounding Sakae skyline lights up, and this naturally means slightly longer queues on weekend nights than on a weekday evening. It's a good option for families with younger kids who might find Midland Square's open-air deck or a taller observation tower intimidating, given the shorter, gentler ride here.
access: Short walk from Sakae Station (Higashiyama and Meijo subway lines)

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Sakae Ferris wheel and shopping pass

title: Horikawa Canal Cherry Blossom Walk
summary: A stretch of Nagoya's old industrial canal that turns into a tunnel of cherry blossoms each spring, walked mostly by locals rather than tour groups.
description:
The Horikawa Canal was dug in the early Edo period to move goods and building materials into the growing castle town, and while its industrial role has faded, several stretches of its banks were later planted with cherry trees that now form a dense, arching canopy for a couple of weeks each spring. Unlike the moat around the castle, this walk is almost entirely a local secret, with the water's stillness reflecting the blossoms in a way that photographs beautifully in the right light.

There's no cost to walk the canal path, and a scenic stretch can be covered in twenty to thirty minutes, though the full canal runs much longer if you want to explore further.

Because it doesn't appear on most tourist maps, even peak bloom rarely brings the crowds seen at Nagoya Castle or the city's larger parks; a weekday walk during the bloom period offers something close to a private cherry-blossom experience. Outside of the short spring window, the canal reverts to a fairly ordinary, quiet waterway, so timing really is everything for this particular spot.
access: Various access points along the canal near Sakae and Marunouchi Station (Sakura-dori subway line)

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Nagoya cherry blossom season tour

title: Nittai-ji Temple
summary: A sect-less Buddhist temple built in 1904 to enshrine a Buddha relic gifted by the King of Siam, still rotating its head priest among 19 different schools of Japanese Buddhism.
description:
Nittai-ji exists because of a diplomatic gift. In the early 1900s a Japanese delegation traveled to Bangkok and received a portion of the Buddha's ashes from King Chulalongkorn, along with an ancient gold-bronze Buddha statue that was itself a Thai national treasure. To house them, the temple's founders built something unusual for Japan: a temple that belongs to no single Buddhist sect. Every few years a different one of the country's nineteen major schools sends its own chief priest to serve here, an arrangement that has held since 1904.

The name itself records the deal: 'Nittai' combines the characters for Japan and Thailand, while 'Kakuo' means 'Enlightenment King,' a reference to the Buddha at the center of the arrangement. The main hall and grounds are modest rather than showy, which suits the neighborhood that grew up around its approach road, but the temple's split allegiance and Thai-gifted relics make it genuinely unlike anywhere else in the city.

Most visitors combine a stop here with a wander through the Kakuozan district that spread out from its front gate over the last century, since the temple itself takes only twenty or thirty minutes to see properly.
access: About a 15-minute walk from Kakuozan Station (Exit 1) on the Higashiyama subway line; Kakuozan Station is about 14 minutes by subway from Nagoya Station with no transfer needed.

title: Kakuozan Sun Road
summary: The old temple-approach street to Nittai-ji, now a low-rise strip of Showa-era shopfronts, indie coffee roasters and a recurring flea market that draws almost no tour buses.
description:
Kakuozan grew up as a monzen-machi, a town that exists to serve pilgrims walking to a temple, in this case Nittai-ji, which was founded in 1904. More than a century later the street that carried those pilgrims is still there, narrower and less polished than Nagoya's big shopping arcades, lined with sweet shops, a public bathhouse or two, and a growing number of small cafes and secondhand bookstores run by people who actually live in the neighborhood.

What makes Kakuozan worth a detour rather than a photo stop is the mix of eras sitting side by side: a decades-old tofu shop next to a natural wine bar, retro apartment blocks with hand-painted signage, and side streets that dead-end into someone's garden. A flea market selling antiques, kimono fabric and secondhand goods sets up along the street on a periodic basis, turning the whole strip into an open-air market for a day.

It rewards slow walking rather than a checklist, and pairs naturally with a stop at Nittai-ji itself or the university-town streets of nearby Yagoto.
access: Directly above Kakuozan Station on the Higashiyama subway line, about 14 minutes from Nagoya Station (no transfer).

title: Kosho-ji Temple, Yagoto
summary: A working Shingon temple whose five-story wooden pagoda is one of the very few left standing anywhere in the Nagoya area.
description:
Yagoto is better known to most visitors as a university district than a temple town, which is exactly why Kosho-ji tends to get skipped. The temple sits on a low rise above the neighborhood's shopping streets, its five-story pagoda visible over the rooftops long before you reach the gate. Multi-story pagodas of this type are rare survivors in a city that lost most of its older wooden architecture to wartime bombing and postwar redevelopment, which makes this one worth the climb even for visitors who have already seen Nagoya's bigger, more famous shrines.

The grounds are quiet on an ordinary weekday: a Kannon hall, stone lanterns, and paths shaded by trees that turn color in late autumn. Because Kosho-ji functions as a working neighborhood temple rather than a tourist attraction, there is no admission fee to walk the grounds and no crowd management to navigate, just the ordinary rhythm of a temple that locals actually use.

Afterward, the surrounding Yagoto area has a dense cluster of cafes and bakeries catering to Nanzan University students, making it easy to turn the visit into a longer, more relaxed afternoon than the temple alone would suggest.
access: About a 3-minute walk from Yagoto Station (Exit 1) on the Meijo subway line, roughly 20 minutes from Nagoya Station with a transfer.

title: Tsuruma Park
summary: Nagoya's oldest public park, centered on a European-style fountain tower from 1910 that survived a subway line being dug straight through the grounds.
description:
Tsuruma Park dates back to 1909 and was the site of a major regional exposition the following year, which is when its centerpiece, a stone-and-marble fountain tower, was first built. Designed by engineer Teiji Suzuki as a deliberate blend of Eastern and Western styles, the tower became one of the park's defining landmarks. It was later dismantled during construction of the Tsurumai subway line and rebuilt in 1983, and it now carries protected status as a municipal cultural property.

The park is one of Nagoya's most reliable seasonal destinations. Cherry trees line the paths in spring and rank among the city's better-known hanami spots, while a Western-style garden on the western side fills with roses in May and June during the park's annual rose festival, and irises follow shortly after in the park's pond areas.

Unlike the manicured formality of some Japanese gardens, Tsuruma Park has the loose, well-used feel of a genuine neighborhood park, with joggers, food stalls during festival weekends and families picnicking under the trees rather than a ticketed, curated experience.
access: Directly above Tsurumai Station, served by both the JR Chuo Line and the Tsurumai subway line, about 10 minutes from Nagoya Station.

title: Shirotori Garden
summary: A modern stroll garden built to compress the entire geography of central Japan, from a mountain source to Ise Bay, into a single 45-minute loop around a koi pond.
description:
Opened in 1991 next to Atsuta Shrine, Shirotori Garden is a chisen-kaiyu-shiki, or pond-and-stroll style, garden designed around a single idea: the journey of water from mountain to sea. A hill near the entrance stands in for Mount Ontake, a stream represents the Kiso River, and the central pond plays the part of Ise Bay, so a full circuit of the garden retraces, in miniature, the landscape that surrounds Nagoya itself.

Within that framework are some genuinely well-crafted details: a sukiya-style teahouse called Seiutei where visitors can have matcha overlooking the pond, and a smaller enclosed section called the Shioiri Garden where the water level rises and falls on an artificial one-hour tidal cycle, mimicking the bay it represents. Around 1,500 Japanese maples and enkianthus shrubs turn the garden into one of the city's better autumn-color spots, usually with far fewer visitors than the more famous gardens near Nagoya Castle.

Because it sits just a few minutes from Atsuta Shrine, Shirotori Garden works well as a quieter second stop after visiting the shrine's busier grounds, offering a very different, more contemplative pace.
access: About a 10-minute walk from Jingu-nishi Station on the Meijo subway line, or a short walk from Atsuta Shrine's southern approach.

title: Arako Kannon Temple
summary: Home to the oldest wooden building still standing in Nagoya, plus one of the country's largest troves of the wandering monk Enku's rough-hewn Buddha carvings.
description:
Arako Kannon, formally Chorin-ji, was founded in the 8th century and grew over the centuries into one of the four major Kannon temples of the Owari region. Its most important structure, a two-story Tahoto pagoda built in 1536, survived the fires and wars that destroyed most of Nagoya's other early wooden buildings, and it now carries designation as a National Important Cultural Property as the oldest wooden structure remaining anywhere in the city. The warlord Maeda Toshiie personally funded repairs to the temple in 1576, a detail that hints at how significant the site once was in the region's power politics; the temple's own main hall was less fortunate, burning down in 1994 and being rebuilt a few years later.

The temple's other claim to fame is its collection of carvings by Enku, a 17th-century itinerant monk who traveled Japan making thousands of deliberately rough, expressive wooden Buddha images. Roughly 1,240 of them ended up here, left to the temple's tenth abbot after Enku stayed at Arako Kannon in 1676, making this one of the largest single collections of his work anywhere in Japan.

The temple sits a short walk from the Endoji shopping street, making the two an easy, low-key pairing on the west side of the station.
access: About an 8-minute walk from Takabata Station (Exit 5, Higashiyama subway line), or about a 10-minute walk from Arako Station (Aonami Line)

title: Nakamura Park and Toyokuni Shrine
summary: A neighborhood park built around the shrine marking the birthplace of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the farmer's son who eventually ruled all of Japan.
description:
Nakamura Ward's claim to fame is that two of the three great unifiers of Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and his fellow general Kato Kiyomasa, are both traditionally said to have been born here as commoners before rising to reshape the country. Toyokuni Shrine, built in the Meiji era on the site associated with Hideyoshi's birth, anchors a small Japanese garden and park where locals walk dogs and eat lunch with little sense that they are standing near the traditional birthplace of a man who once ruled the entire country.

The shrine buildings themselves are modest compared to Nagoya's grander religious sites, but the historical weight of the location, a warlord's son born into farming poverty who ended up unifying Japan, gives the visit more resonance than the architecture alone suggests. A small museum-style hall nearby displays material related to Hideyoshi's life and career for visitors who want more context.

It is a five-minute detour rather than a half-day destination, best combined with a walk through the surrounding Nakamura neighborhood or a stop at nearby Arako Kannon.
access: About a 10-minute walk from Exit 3 of Nakamura-koen Station on the Higashiyama subway line, roughly 15 minutes from Nagoya Station.

title: Cultural Path Shumokukan
summary: A quieter Taisho-era merchant residence a short walk from the Futaba Museum, offering the same Japanese-Western hybrid architecture with far fewer visitors.
description:
The Bunka no Michi district was, in the Edo period, a row of samurai residences serving the Owari domain; by the Meiji and Taisho eras it had become home to a new class of businessmen, journalists and public figures who built mansions blending imported Western style with traditional Japanese construction. Shumokukan is one of the surviving examples of that transition, a merchant family's residence whose rooms alternate between Japanese tatami spaces and Western-style parlors with imported furniture and detailing.

Compared to the Futaba Museum a short walk away, Shumokukan tends to draw a fraction of the visitors, which makes it a good place to actually take in the architectural details, the garden, and the layout of a wealthy household from a century ago without navigating a crowd. Admission is inexpensive and the building can be seen thoroughly in well under an hour.

Walking between Shumokukan and the Futaba Museum, along streets still lined with older houses and small gardens, is arguably the best way to experience the Cultural Path district as a whole rather than as a single stop.
access: About a 10-minute walk from Exit 1 of Takaoka Station on the Sakuradori subway line, close to the Futaba Museum.

title: Higashiyama Sky Tower
summary: A 100-meter observation tower rising from a hill inside the Higashiyama Zoo grounds, built for Nagoya's centennial and ranked among Japan's top night views.
description:
Built in 1989 to mark the hundredth anniversary of Nagoya's founding, the Higashiyama Sky Tower stands on top of an already elevated hill within the Higashiyama Zoo and Botanical Gardens, putting its observation deck roughly 180 meters above sea level even though the tower structure itself rises about 100 meters. On a clear day the deck offers views across the Nagoya TV Tower and Nagoya Dome, out toward Mount Ontake on the Gifu border, and as far as the Suzuka mountains in Mie, a panorama that has earned the tower recognition as one of Japan's top night-view destinations.

A restaurant on the uppermost floor serves casual Italian and French food for lunch and a more formal menu in the evening, making the tower a workable dinner-with-a-view option rather than just a daytime lookout. Because it sits inside the wider Higashiyama Park complex, which also holds Nagoya's main zoo and botanical garden, a visit here is easy to fold into a longer day in the area rather than a special trip on its own.

The tower gets a fraction of the visitor numbers of Nagoya's more famous downtown observation points, largely because it requires a subway ride out to Higashiyama Koen rather than a stop in the city center.
access: About a 15-minute walk from Exit 3 of Higashiyama Koen Station on the Higashiyama subway line, roughly 20 minutes from Nagoya Station.

title: Nanatsudera Temple
summary: A temple older than Nagoya itself, physically relocated from Kiyosu when the city was founded and now standing quietly just off Osu's busier arcades.
description:
Nanatsudera was originally built in 735 in what is now Ama City, west of Nagoya, long before Nagoya existed as a city. It was later moved to Kiyosu in 1591, and when Tokugawa Ieyasu ordered the construction of Nagoya Castle in the early 1600s, he also ordered much of the population and many institutions of Kiyosu, including several temples and shrines, physically moved to the new castle town in an event known locally as the Kiyosu-goshi. Nanatsudera was relocated to its current site in Osu in 1611 as part of that process, making it one of the oldest continuously operating religious institutions in the city even though its current site is comparatively young.

Under the Owari branch of the Tokugawa family, the temple served as an important place of worship and hosted lively festivals throughout the Edo period, drawing crowds from across the growing castle town. Today it sits within walking distance of the far busier Osu Kannon temple and shopping arcade, but it keeps a much lower profile, visited mostly by neighborhood residents rather than tour groups.

It makes a natural, low-effort addition to a visit to the Osu district, offering a quieter historical counterpoint to the shopping and street food a few minutes away.
access: About a 5-minute walk from Kamimaezu Station on the Meijo or Tsurumai subway lines.

title: Nagoya City Archives
summary: A neo-baroque red-brick former Court of Appeals building whose marble staircases and vacated courtrooms now hold Nagoya's municipal historical records.
description:
Completed in 1922, this building served for decades as Nagoya's court of appeals along with a local and district court, functioning as the judiciary center for the greater Chubu region until the courts moved to a new facility in 1979. A decade later the vacated building was converted into the Nagoya City Archives, tasked with preserving and making public the city's official historical documents, a role it still holds today.

Architecturally, the building is a striking example of early twentieth-century Western-influenced design, its neo-baroque facade combining red brick with white granite trim in a style that was fashionable in Japan during the Taisho era. Only two Court of Appeals buildings from this design lineage survive in Japan, this one and a counterpart in Sapporo, and the Nagoya building has been designated a National Important Cultural Property as a result. Inside, the restored marble staircase, meeting rooms and a preserved courtroom give a strong sense of the building's original judicial function even though its purpose has completely changed.

It sits within the Bunka no Michi Cultural Path district, making it easy to combine with a visit to the nearby Futaba Museum and Shumokukan.
access: About an 8-minute walk from Exit 2 of Nagoya-jo Station on the Meijo subway line.

title: Antarctic Research Ship Fuji
summary: A retired Antarctic icebreaker permanently docked at Nagoya Port, its crew quarters and helicopter deck preserved exactly as they were on its last polar voyage.
description:
The Fuji spent eighteen years breaking ice for Japan's Antarctic research program after its first voyage south in 1965, a bright orange-and-white vessel about 100 meters long capable of pushing through ice up to 80 centimeters thick. When it was finally retired, the ship was towed to Nagoya Port in 1985 rather than scrapped, and it has sat in the Garden Wharf area, opposite the Nagoya Port Aquarium, as a floating museum ever since, complete with a Sikorsky Sea King helicopter still parked on its rear deck.

What sets the Fuji apart from a typical maritime museum is how much of the working ship was left intact rather than converted into display cases. Visitors can walk through crew bunks, the ship's barber shop, the mess hall and other functional spaces exactly as they were used, which gives a much more visceral sense of what eighteen years of Antarctic service actually looked like day to day than a set of photographs would.

It is an easy, inexpensive add-on to a visit to the aquarium and port area, and a good option for families traveling with kids who want something more hands-on than a standard museum.
access: About a 5-minute walk from Nagoyako Station on the Meiko subway line.

title: SKE48 Theater
summary: The dedicated live-performance theater of idol group SKE48, tucked into the second floor of a Sakae shopping complex since its first show in 2008.
description:
SKE48 takes its name directly from Sakae, Nagoya's central entertainment and shopping district, making it the local sister group in the wider AKB48 franchise model of city-based idol groups performing in their own dedicated theaters. The Nagoya theater opened inside the Sunshine Sakae complex and held its first performance in October 2008, launching with a founding lineup that became the group's original Team S.

The group has since grown into a multi-team structure, with members performing regularly in rotating theater shows that mix choreographed pop numbers with more casual talk segments, a format that has become the standard for this style of Japanese idol group. Tickets are usually allocated through a lottery system aimed at dedicated fans rather than casual walk-ins, so visitors hoping to catch a show should check the schedule and ticket process well in advance rather than showing up on the day.

Even without attending a performance, the theater and its surrounding merchandise shop give a concentrated look at a specific corner of Japanese pop culture that most sightseeing itineraries never touch.
access: Inside Sunshine Sakae, about a 3-minute walk from Sakae Station on the Higashiyama or Meijo subway lines.

title: Sunshine Sakae Sky-Boat Ferris Wheel
summary: A candy-colored Ferris wheel bolted onto the roof of a Sakae shopping complex, offering one of the more unexpected skyline views in central Nagoya.
description:
Rather than standing on the ground like most Ferris wheels, the Sky-Boat sits directly on top of the Sunshine Sakae shopping and entertainment complex, functioning as the building's unmistakable visual signature from street level. Riders board from an upper floor of the complex and circle above the rooftops of Sakae, Nagoya's densest entertainment district, with sightlines toward the Nagoya TV Tower, the greenery of Hisaya-odori Park, and the wider grid of the city center.

At night the wheel is lit in changing colors, adding to Sakae's already bright evening atmosphere and making it a popular, if slightly kitschy, photo subject from the streets below. The ride itself is short and inexpensive, more of a novelty stop than a major attraction, but the elevated, close-up view of a working entertainment district is different from what taller, more famous observation decks in the city offer.

It pairs naturally with a visit to the SKE48 Theater in the same building, or with an evening out exploring Sakae's restaurants and bars.
access: Inside Sunshine Sakae, about a 3-minute walk from Sakae Station on the Higashiyama or Meijo subway lines.

title: Toganji Temple
summary: A suburban temple guarded by a 10-meter green-and-gold Buddha perched on ten bronze elephants, with a small Hindu shrine tucked into its grounds.
description:
Toganji was founded in the mid-1500s by Oda Nobuyuki in memory of his father Oda Nobuhide, taking part of its name from Nobuhide's posthumous Buddhist title. The temple later relocated to its present site in the Moriyama area in the early 1700s, where it has remained ever since as a working Soto Zen temple focused on the bodhisattva Kannon.

Its most striking feature by far is a modern addition: a roughly 10-meter bronze Buddha statue, unveiled in 1987 and supported by ten sculpted elephants, painted in vivid green with gold-leaf accents that make it visible well before you reach the temple gate. The statue reflects a broader Indian connection at Toganji, whose grounds also include a small shrine to Saraswati and a Shiva lingam, unusual additions traced back to a former high priest who studied Buddhism in India. An annual festival honoring Saraswati, known in Japan as Benzaiten, is held on the temple grounds each spring.

Toganji sits well outside the usual downtown temple circuit, which keeps it free of tour groups even though its giant Buddha is genuinely one of the more photogenic religious statues in the greater Nagoya area.
access: Near Motoyama Station on the Meijo or Higashiyama subway lines, in Chikusa-ku.

title: Nagoya City Museum
summary: Nagoya's main history museum, holding the country's oldest boat-shaped wooden coffin alongside armor and artifacts tied to hometown warlords Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi.
description:
Opened in 1977 to mark Nagoya's population passing two million, the Nagoya City Museum sits inside Mizuho Park and functions as the city's primary institution for the history and culture of both Nagoya and the wider Aichi region. Its holdings run to hundreds of thousands of items, from archaeological finds of the Jomon and Yayoi periods, including the oldest known boat-shaped wooden coffin in Japan, through to roof tiles and Buddhist images from the Nara and Heian eras.

The permanent exhibition traces local history from the Paleolithic period to the present day, with particular attention paid to the two warlords most closely associated with the Nagoya area, Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and to the subsequent rise of the Owari branch of the Tokugawa family that ruled the region for over two centuries. A rotating program of special exhibitions throughout the year covers everything from specific cultural-heritage topics to broader themes in Owari regional history.

As with any large municipal museum, it is worth checking current opening status and any renovation schedule before visiting, since exhibition halls occasionally close for extended maintenance.
access: About a 5-minute walk from Sakurayama Station on the Meijo subway line.

title: Urakuen Garden and Joan Teahouse
summary: A national-treasure teahouse built for Oda Nobunaga's tea-master brother, relocated twice across Japan before settling in this quiet garden beside Inuyama Castle.
description:
The teahouse at the heart of Urakuen Garden, known as Joan, was built around 1618 for Oda Urakusai, a younger brother of Oda Nobunaga and a disciple of the legendary tea master Sen no Rikyu. It originally stood at Kennin-ji temple in Kyoto and is regarded as one of the three finest surviving teahouses in Japan, a status confirmed when it was designated a National Treasure in 1951. Over the following decades the structure was relocated first to Tokyo and then to Kanagawa before finally settling in Inuyama in 1972, just east of the castle.

Joan is a study in deliberate restraint: a low wooden-shingle roof, walls of clay-covered bamboo lattice, and a tiny crawl-through entrance called a nijiriguchi designed to strip away rank and formality before guests enter the two-and-a-half-tatami tea room inside. The garden surrounding it was laid out to complement that same understated aesthetic, with stone paths and plantings meant to be experienced slowly rather than photographed in passing.

Because the teahouse itself is generally viewed from outside rather than entered, a visit here is more about the garden setting and the history behind the structure than a hands-on tea ceremony, though seasonal tea events are sometimes held on the grounds.
access: About a 10-minute walk from Inuyama Yuen Station on the Meitetsu line, roughly 30 minutes from Nagoya.

title: Festival Museum Dondenkan
summary: A pocket-sized museum keeping Inuyama's elaborate festival floats on permanent display, for travelers who can't time a visit to the single-day spring festival itself.
description:
The Inuyama Festival, held on the first Saturday of April, is one of the region's major float festivals, with elaborately decorated Yama floats pulled through the streets of the castle town in a display of lacquerwork, gold foil and fine woodcarving. For the rest of the year, when the floats are in storage, the Dondenkan museum offers the only way to see them up close, displaying four of the festival's Yama floats inside a compact, narrow-fronted building styled after the traditional castle-town merchant houses that once lined the street outside.

A short light-and-sound presentation inside recreates the atmosphere of festival day in a few minutes, giving a reasonable sense of the event's scale and energy without the crowds. A separate display case holds the ornate gold-embroidered garments, known as kinjuban, worn by children who take part in the festival procession, offering a closer look at details that are easy to miss amid the noise of the real event.

Admission is inexpensive, and the museum takes well under an hour to see properly, making it a natural stop on the walk between Inuyama Castle and Urakuen Garden.
access: About an 8 to 10-minute walk from Inuyama Station on the Meitetsu line, near the base of Inuyama Castle.

title: Inuyama Castle Town, Honmachi-dori
summary: The old main street of Inuyama's castle town, its Edo and Meiji-era merchant houses now selling grilled gohei-mochi and local sake instead of samurai supplies.
description:
Honmachi-dori runs in a straight line from the base of Inuyama Castle down through the old jokamachi, or castle town, that grew up to serve it. Many of the wooden storefronts lining the street date from the Edo period through the early twentieth century, their narrow frontages and deep interiors a classic layout for merchant houses of the era, and a fair number are still occupied by shops selling exactly the kinds of goods, sake, sweets, pottery, that their predecessors might have sold generations ago.

What makes the street especially good for a slow visit is its street-food culture: stalls and small shopfronts sell gohei-mochi, a grilled rice cake coated in a sweet-savory miso or soy glaze that is something of a local specialty, along with skewered snacks and cups of sake from breweries in the surrounding region, meant to be eaten while strolling rather than sitting down. The street angles gently uphill toward the castle, so the walk builds naturally toward the day's main destination.

Because it connects directly to the castle, Urakuen Garden and the Dondenkan museum, Honmachi-dori works as much as connective tissue as it does a destination of its own, but it rewards visitors who slow down rather than walk straight through.
access: About a 15-minute walk from Inuyama Station, or a 12 to 15-minute walk from Inuyama Yuen Station on the Meitetsu line.

title: Museum Meiji-Mura
summary: An open-air museum where more than sixty real Meiji and Taisho-era buildings, including the entrance lobby of Frank Lloyd Wright's original Imperial Hotel, were dismantled elsewhere and rebuilt beside a lake.
description:
Meiji-mura opened in 1965 with a specific mission: to rescue architecturally significant buildings from Japan's rapid modernization, roughly the Meiji, Taisho and early Showa periods, before they were demolished and lost entirely. Over the decades since, more than sixty structures have been physically relocated here and reassembled across a sprawling, hilly site beside Lake Iruka, with eleven of them now designated Important Cultural Properties and most of the rest registered as Tangible Cultural Properties.

The collection's centerpiece is the reconstructed entrance hall and lobby of Frank Lloyd Wright's original Imperial Hotel, which stood in Tokyo from 1923 until the main building was demolished in 1967 to make way for a larger replacement; this fragment is the closest most visitors will ever get to experiencing Wright's original design. Elsewhere on the grounds are Lafcadio Hearn's summer house, a Meiji-era Christian church designed by James McDonald Gardiner, and Kyoto's old St. Francis Xavier Catholic Cathedral, alongside buildings imported from as far away as Hawaii, Seattle and Brazil.

The site is large enough that a thorough visit takes most of a day, with a vintage steam locomotive and old Kyoto trams running between distant sections to help visitors cover the ground.
access: Meitetsu bus from Inuyama Station, about 20 minutes; the museum is roughly 40 to 50 minutes total from central Nagoya.

title: Little World Museum of Man
summary: A sprawling open-air museum where villages from more than twenty countries, some rebuilt from original materials, sit within walking distance of each other along a single trail.
description:
Founded in 1983 as an anthropological open-air park (the concept originated around the 1970 Osaka Expo), Little World takes a different approach from Japan's more common single-country heritage museums by recreating traditional dwellings and village life from more than twenty countries across a single site. A roughly 2.5-kilometer walking route connects 33 structures representing everyday architecture from places as varied as Peru, India, Germany and Thailand, with some buildings faithfully reconstructed to local specifications and others relocated using genuine original materials.

An indoor exhibition hall supplements the outdoor village walk with around 6,000 cultural artifacts drawn from roughly 70 countries, covering clothing, tools and everyday objects that don't fit neatly into a single reconstructed building. Visitors can rent traditional outfits from several of the represented cultures for photos, and restaurants scattered along the route serve dishes loosely tied to the regions they sit near, from Indian curry to Peruvian folk-craft-adjacent snacks.

It is a substantial site best paired with a full day rather than a quick stop, and works well as a joint outing with nearby Meiji-mura for visitors focused on architecture and world cultures rather than castles and gardens.
access: Meitetsu bus from Inuyama Station, about 20 to 25 minutes; roughly 45 to 60 minutes total from central Nagoya.

title: Japan Monkey Park
summary: A hillside combination zoo and old-school amusement park overlooking the Kiso River, anchored by the world-renowned Japan Monkey Centre's primate collection.
description:
Japan Monkey Park occupies a wooded hillside above the Kiso River, combining a genuinely significant zoological institution with a fairly conventional Japanese amusement park under one admission ticket. The zoological half, the Japan Monkey Centre, holds one of the largest primate collections on earth, with dozens of species and several hundred individual animals spanning macaques, gibbons, lemurs and great apes from Asia, Africa and the Americas.

Its best-known attraction is Monkey Valley, where visitors can watch Japanese macaques wash sweet potatoes in a running stream, a learned behavior first documented in wild macaque populations decades ago and now considered an example of animal culture being passed between generations. On the amusement park side, a day pass typically covers a set number of rides, including roller coasters, a Ferris wheel and gentler attractions for younger children, with a pool in summer and an ice rink in winter rounding out the seasonal offerings.

It is a good match for families who want more active entertainment than a castle or museum visit offers, without leaving the Inuyama area.
access: About a 5-minute bus ride from the east exit of Inuyama Station on the Meitetsu line.

title: Tokoname Pottery Footpath (Yakimono Sanpomichi)
summary: A hillside walking course through six centuries of pottery-making, past kiln chimneys and a three-meter lucky cat peeking over a brick embankment.
description:
Tokoname is counted among Japan's Six Ancient Kilns, a group of pottery-producing regions with continuous production histories stretching back roughly a thousand years, and the Yakimono Sanpomichi, or Pottery Footpath, is the most direct way to experience that history on foot. The shorter of its two marked routes, Course A, covers about 1.6 kilometers through the old kiln district, passing brick chimneys, working studios and small galleries selling Tokoname-yaki ceramics.

The route's signature stretch is Dokan-zaka, a sloped lane paved with old clay pipes and ceramic jars set on their sides into the ground, creating one of the most photographed textures in the region. Nearby, Maneki Neko-dori, or Lucky Cat Street, is lined with dozens of Tokoname-made beckoning cat statues, a nod to the city's status as Japan's largest producer of maneki-neko, and the street culminates in Tokonyan, a roughly three-meter-tall cat face and paw emerging from an embankment, one of the largest lucky cat figures in the country.

The walk is compact enough to complete in an hour or two, making Tokoname an easy half-day trip that pairs naturally with the nearby INAX Live Museum.
access: Meitetsu train from Nagoya to Tokoname Station, about 30 minutes, then a short walk to the start of the footpath.

title: INAX Live Museum
summary: A cluster of galleries and preserved brick kilns run by tile-maker LIXIL, tracing everything from ancient roof tiles to the ceramics of world architecture.
description:
Run by the building-materials company LIXIL under its INAX tile brand, the INAX Live Museum is really a small campus of separate exhibition spaces built around Tokoname's identity as a ceramics town. A preserved noborigama, or climbing kiln, along with a tall brick chimney once used for firing terracotta pipes, anchors the outdoor section, giving visitors a close look at the industrial-scale kiln technology that powered the region's pottery trade for over a century.

Indoors, separate galleries cover the history of roof tiles across Japan, decorative architectural ceramics from around the world, and the broader story of how clay has been used in construction from ancient times to the present. Hands-on workshops let visitors try their hand at basic clay work, making the museum a reasonable stop for families as well as design and architecture enthusiasts.

The museum sits close enough to the Yakimono Sanpomichi pottery footpath that the two make an obvious pairing for a half-day in Tokoname focused on ceramics.
access: About a 25 to 30-minute walk from Tokoname Station on the Meitetsu line, or a roughly 6-minute bus ride (Chita Bus) followed by a short walk, or a short taxi ride.

title: Arimatsu Historic Townscape
summary: An 800-meter stretch of the old Tokaido highway where merchant houses that grew wealthy on tie-dyed cloth still stand largely unchanged since the Edo period.
description:
Arimatsu was established in 1608 under an official decree from the Owari Tokugawa domain, positioned along the Tokaido, the great highway linking Edo and Kyoto, specifically to serve travelers passing through. According to local tradition, workers brought in from Bungo province to help build Nagoya Castle carried with them a tie-dyeing technique that a local merchant recognized as commercially promising, and by the 1630s Arimatsu's shibori cloth trade was firmly established, sold to travelers as a specialty souvenir of the road.

That trade made the town genuinely prosperous, and the merchant houses built with the proceeds, many dating from the late Edo period through the early Showa era, still line roughly 800 meters of the old highway today. A number of these buildings carry official Tangible Cultural Heritage designation, and the townscape as a whole gives one of the clearer pictures of what a Tokaido post town actually looked like, without the heavy restoration and souvenir-shop conversion seen at some more famous historic streets.

More than a hundred distinct shibori tying techniques are still practiced by craftspeople connected to the town, several of which are demonstrated at the nearby Shibori Kaikan museum.
access: Meitetsu train from Nagoya to Arimatsu Station, about 25 minutes.

title: Arimatsu-Narumi Shibori Kaikan
summary: A hands-on museum inside a historic Arimatsu house where working tie-dye artisans demonstrate their technique in real time, upstairs from a shop selling the finished cloth.
description:
Opened in 1984 to help pass Arimatsu's shibori tie-dyeing tradition on to future generations, this museum splits its historic building into a straightforward ground-floor shop selling finished shibori textiles and a more hands-on second floor dedicated to the craft itself. There, working artisans demonstrate kukuri, the painstaking hand-tying process that creates shibori's distinctive patterns, in open view of visitors for most of the day, pausing only for a lunch break.

A short film gives an overview of the full production process, from carving the pattern and transferring it to cloth, through tying, dyeing and finally removing the stitches, a sequence that can take a single piece of cloth weeks to complete depending on its complexity. For visitors who want to go further than watching, the museum offers a reservation-based hands-on experience where guests tie their own piece of fabric, which is then dyed and shipped to them afterward.

Because it sits directly on the old Tokaido townscape, the museum is easy to combine with a walk through the rest of historic Arimatsu.
access: About a 5-minute walk from Arimatsu Station on the Meitetsu line.

title: Kamagaki no Komichi
summary: A winding lane found nowhere else in Japan, its walls and fences built from centuries of discarded kiln tools instead of brick or stone.
description:
For generations, potters in Seto's old Hora district built up the walls, fences and foundations around their homes and workshops using worn-out kiln furniture, the saggars, supports and firing tools that wear out through repeated use and get discarded, rather than buying conventional building materials. Over time this practical habit produced Kamagaki no Komichi, a lane running nearly 400 meters where discarded kiln tools have been stacked into genuinely distinctive walls, a sight unique to this one street in Seto.

The lane itself follows what was once a main route for moving finished pottery through the town, and it is still lined with the homes of kiln-owning families along with small studios and galleries selling contemporary Seto ware. A gallery inside a converted late-Meiji-era kiln sits partway along the route, occasionally hosting local festivals where residents sell original pottery pieces and serve simple seasonal food to visitors.

Seto itself, one of Japan's Six Ancient Kilns and the origin of the generic Japanese word for ceramics, seto-mono, rarely appears on first-time Nagoya itineraries, which makes this walk feel like a genuine discovery rather than a checklist stop.
access: Meitetsu Seto Line from Sakae to Owari-Seto Station, about 32 to 37 minutes depending on train type, then a short walk into the Hora district.

title: Aichi Prefectural Ceramic Museum
summary: A prefectural museum set in wooded hills outside Seto, tracing the full sweep of Japanese ceramics with particular depth on the local Seto-Mino kiln tradition.
description:
Located in the hills of Seto, roughly 20 kilometers northeast of central Nagoya, the Aichi Prefectural Ceramic Museum surveys the history of Japanese ceramics with a natural emphasis on the Seto and Mino kiln traditions that developed in this immediate area over the past thousand years. Its collection spans everyday utilitarian wares through to refined tea ceramics, giving visitors a broader technical and historical context than the smaller craft-focused stops elsewhere in Seto.

The museum's setting is part of its appeal: rather than a downtown building, it occupies a quiet, forested campus that changes with the seasons, making the walk between its buildings as pleasant as the exhibits themselves. Because it is a prefectural rather than municipal institution, it periodically hosts larger touring or thematic exhibitions in addition to its permanent collection.

Getting there requires a bit more effort than Seto's central pottery district, via the Linimo maglev line, which makes it a good option for visitors who want a quieter, more scholarly ceramics stop after the busier lanes of central Seto or Tokoname.
access: Linimo maglev line from Fujigaoka Station to Tojishiryokan-Minami Station, then about an 8 to 10-minute walk.

title: Kiyosu Castle
summary: A concrete reconstruction of the castle where a young Oda Nobunaga plotted his rise, built on the site his own crews later stripped to construct Nagoya Castle.
description:
Kiyosu Castle was originally built in the early 1400s to guard the junction of two major highways, and it grew into a genuinely important stronghold once Oda Nobunaga retook it in 1555 and used it as his base during the years he consolidated power over Owari Province. It was at Kiyosu that Nobunaga formalized his alliance with Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1562, a partnership that would shape the following century of Japanese history, before Nobunaga himself relocated to Komaki and later Gifu.

The castle's original buildings did not survive Nobunaga's own successors: between 1609 and 1613, much of Kiyosu Castle was deliberately dismantled so its materials could be reused in the construction of the new Nagoya Castle a short distance away, part of a broader relocation of the region's political center. By the Meiji era almost nothing remained beyond earthworks, and the Tokaido rail line was eventually built directly across part of the old castle grounds.

The reinforced-concrete keep visitors see today dates only from 1989, built to mark the modern town's centennial and modeled loosely on Inuyama Castle's donjon rather than reconstructed from Kiyosu's own original plans, so it should be understood as a commemorative structure rather than a historically accurate rebuild.
access: JR Tokaido Line from Nagoya Station to Kiyosu Station, about 10 minutes, then about a 15-minute walk, or a shorter bus ride.

title: Komaki Castle
summary: A hilltop ruin where Oda Nobunaga pioneered the stone-walled castle-town template later perfected at Azuchi, with a modern lookout on top offering wide Nobi Plain views.
description:
Oda Nobunaga built Komaki Castle in 1563, his third castle after Nagoya and Kiyosu, choosing a solitary 86-meter hill north of the Nagoya area for its commanding view over the flat Nobi Plain during his campaign against the Saito clan of neighboring Mino Province. What made Komaki historically significant was not its size but its design: it was among the first Japanese castles to make extensive use of stacked-stone defensive walls, arranged in concentric rings around the summit, a technique that would later be refined into the more famous stonework of Nobunaga's later castle at Azuchi.

Komaki also broke new ground by pairing the hilltop fortress with a purpose-built castle town laid out below it and partially protected by moats and earthen walls, an early example of the administrative-residential castle-town model that later became standard across Japan. Nobunaga abandoned Komaki as his main base in 1567 after defeating the Saito and moving on to Gifu, but the site saw renewed military significance in 1584 during the Komaki-Nagakute campaign between Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu.

Today the hill is a public park topped by a small history museum and observation hall, with walking paths through the old stone-wall remains for visitors willing to climb.
access: Meitetsu Komaki Line from Nagoya to Komaki Station, about 25 minutes, then a bus or roughly 20-minute walk to the hill.

title: Konomiya Shrine and the Hadaka Matsuri
summary: The Owari region's biggest naked festival, where thousands of loincloth-clad men chase a single chosen man through the shrine grounds to transfer their bad luck onto him.
description:
Konomiya Shrine, formally Owari Okunitama Shrine, traces the origins of its most famous rite back to the year 767, when the governor of Owari Province is said to have come here to pray for relief from a spreading epidemic on imperial orders. That ritual survives today as the Hadaka Matsuri, or Naked Festival, held on the thirteenth day of the old lunar calendar, typically falling in February.

On the day of the festival, thousands of men wearing only white loincloths and headbands converge on the shrine grounds in a ritual meant to drive out disease and misfortune. At the center of the event is the shin-otoko, or 'lucky man,' a young local man chosen for the role who runs through the crowd completely naked; participants believe that touching him transfers their own bad luck onto him, and the resulting crush of thousands of men chasing a single runner is one of the more physically intense festival experiences in Japan.

Outside of the festival itself, Konomiya Shrine functions as a fairly typical, quiet Shinto shrine, so visitors hoping to see the Hadaka Matsuri in person need to plan their trip specifically around its date each year.
access: Meitetsu Nagoya Main Line from Nagoya to Konomiya Station, about 20 minutes, then a short walk.

title: Hatcho Miso Village
summary: Two rival miso breweries that have faced off across the same stretch of the old Tokaido road for close to four centuries, still aging soybean miso in giant cedar barrels topped with river stones.
description:
The name Hatcho Miso comes directly from this small district of Okazaki, home to two long-running miso breweries, Maruya and Kakukyu, that between them have shaped the identity of Aichi's distinctive dark, richly savory soybean miso. Maruya traces its history back to 1337, while Kakukyu began commercial production in 1645, though its founding family's involvement in miso-making reaches back further, to a samurai retainer who reportedly gave up his warrior life after the Battle of Okehazama and settled here to learn the trade.

Both breweries still flank the old Tokaido highway, Maruya on one side and Kakukyu on the other, and both offer factory tours that walk visitors past rows of massive wooden barrels, some of them generations old, each topped with a carefully stacked pyramid of river stones used to weigh down the fermenting miso over a two-year aging process. The traditional method has changed remarkably little since the Edo period, and tour guides are generally happy to explain the physics behind the stone-stacking technique in detail.

Both breweries run small shops selling their miso and miso-based snacks at the end of the tour, making this an easy, food-focused stop on the way to or from Okazaki Castle.
access: About a 1-minute walk from Okazaki-koen-mae Station on the Meitetsu Nagoya Main Line, roughly 35 to 40 minutes from Nagoya (Higashi Okazaki Station, sometimes cited, is actually about a 20-25 minute walk away).

title: Okazaki Castle
summary: The castle where Tokugawa Ieyasu was born in 1543, rebuilt in concrete in 1959 after Meiji-era demolition left only its stone foundations standing.
description:
The site of Okazaki Castle dates back to a modest fortification built in 1455, later taken over and relocated a short distance by the Matsudaira clan in 1526. It was here, in 1543, that Tokugawa Ieyasu was born as Matsudaira Takechiyo, decades before he would go on to unify Japan and found the Tokugawa shogunate that ruled the country for the next two and a half centuries. Ieyasu's own time at the castle was brief and interrupted; he was sent away as a child hostage at age six and, though he returned at nineteen, relocated his base to Hamamatsu Castle roughly a decade later.

Following Ieyasu's victory at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Okazaki Castle passed into the hands of Tokugawa vassals, who held it until the Meiji Restoration. The new Meiji government ordered the castle demolished in 1873, leaving only foundation stones, moats and stone walls, a fate shared by many Japanese castles during that period of rapid modernization. The current keep is a 1959 reconstruction built in the original style and scale, along with an annex and well house.

The surrounding park is one of the region's popular cherry-blossom spots each spring, and a small museum inside the keep covers Ieyasu's life and the broader Sengoku-era history connected to the site.
access: Meitetsu train from Nagoya to Higashi Okazaki Station, about 35 to 40 minutes, then about a 15-minute walk.

title: Nishio, the Matcha Town
summary: A quiet river town that produces roughly a fifth of Japan's tencha, the shade-grown leaf that becomes matcha, its fields still covered by the same straw shading racks used since the early twentieth century.
description:
Tea cultivation in Nishio dates back to 1271, when the founder of a local temple is said to have first planted tea seeds here, but the town's specific focus on matcha developed much later, expanding significantly from the late Taisho era onward as growers shifted toward the shade-cultivation techniques that produce tencha, the specially grown leaf ground into matcha powder. Today Nishio accounts for roughly a fifth of all tencha produced in Japan, standing alongside Kyoto's Uji as one of the country's two historically defining matcha regions, even though it remains far less known to overseas visitors.

The surrounding countryside, where the Yahagi River meets Mikawa Bay, is dotted with tea fields still shaded using traditional straw and cloth racks during the weeks before harvest, a technique that concentrates chlorophyll and amino acids in the leaf and produces matcha's characteristic vivid green color and umami-forward flavor. Several tea companies and small workshops in town offer hands-on matcha experiences, letting visitors grind leaf by hand with a traditional stone mortar and prepare their own bowl of tea in a simple tearoom setting.

The grounds of the former Nishio Castle, now a public park in the town center, make a pleasant, unhurried base for a day built around tea rather than monuments.
access: Meitetsu train from Nagoya to Nishio Station, about 50 to 60 minutes with a transfer.

title: MIZKAN MUSEUM (MIM)
summary: A vinegar company's own museum along a black-walled Edo canal, where visitors can climb aboard a full-scale replica of the sailing ship that once carried its product to Edo.
description:
The Mizkan Group's history begins in 1804, when a sake brewer named Matazaemon Nakano succeeded in producing vinegar from leftover sake lees, a byproduct that had previously gone to waste, launching what would eventually become one of Japan's largest vinegar producers. The company's own museum, known as MIM, sits directly on the Handa Canal that once carried its barrels of vinegar, along with sake and cotton from across the Chita Peninsula, out to Edo and the Kamigata region during the Edo period.

The museum is organized into five themed zones tracing that journey from the early nineteenth century to the present, walking visitors through traditional brewing techniques inside a recreated 'Room of Earth' before letting them climb aboard a full-scale, 20-meter reconstruction of a bezai-style sailing ship, the type of vessel that once carried Mizkan's vinegar barrels on the multi-week voyage to Edo. The setting itself, with the canal's aged black-walled warehouses still standing outside, does as much to convey the history as the exhibits inside.

A combined ticket covering MIM and the nearby Kunizakari Sake Museum is a reasonable way to see two of Handa's brewing traditions in a single afternoon.
access: About a 3-minute walk from Handa Station on the JR Taketoyo Line, roughly 35 to 40 minutes from Nagoya.

title: Handa Canal and Kuranomachi Storehouse District
summary: A row of black-walled Edo-period storehouses lining a narrow canal, the same waterway that once floated the Chita Peninsula's sake and vinegar barrels toward Tokyo.
description:
The Handa Canal was dug during the Edo period specifically to move goods, chiefly sake, vinegar and cotton produced on the Chita Peninsula, out to the major markets of Edo and the Kamigata region around Kyoto and Osaka. That trade made Handa genuinely prosperous, and much of the wealth went into the tall, black-walled storehouses that still line the canal today, their weathered wooden siding and white-plaster trim largely unchanged since brewers used them to age and store barrels before shipment.

Walking the canal now means passing several still-operating breweries alongside the storehouses, including buildings connected to the Mizkan vinegar company and to sake producers whose names have been attached to this stretch of water for generations. In the evening, when the storehouses are lit and reflected in the still canal water, the district becomes one of the more photogenic streetscapes in the Nagoya day-trip radius, with almost none of the crowds that gather at more famous preserved townscapes elsewhere in Japan.

It sits close enough to the MIZKAN MUSEUM that the two can easily be combined into a single, walkable afternoon in Handa.
access: About a 10-minute walk from Handa Station on the JR Taketoyo Line, roughly 40 minutes from Nagoya.

title: Tsushima Shrine
summary: The head shrine of roughly three thousand branch shrines across Japan, ranked alongside Kyoto's Yasaka Shrine and famous for a summer festival of lantern-lit boats.
description:
Tsushima Shrine's own history stretches back to the year 540, making it one of the older continuously operating shrines in the region, and it grew over the centuries into the head shrine of a network of roughly three thousand branch shrines spread across Japan, all connected to the worship of the deity Gozu Tenno, historically understood as a protector against plague and epidemic disease. That rank places Tsushima Shrine on a level with Kyoto's famous Yasaka Shrine, its counterpart in the same religious tradition, even though it remains far less visited by international travelers.

The shrine's biggest event, the Tsushima Tenno Festival, unfolds over an evening and the following morning in late July and counts among Japan's three great river festivals. On the first night, five boats laden with lanterns and playing traditional Tsushima flute music drift down the Tenno River from a nearby pond, their lights reflected on the water in a scene that has drawn visitors for centuries. The following morning brings six more elaborately decorated boats, this time carrying men who leap into the river and swim ashore carrying banner-adorned pikes as an offering at the shrine.

Outside festival dates, the shrine grounds themselves are calm and unhurried, making a good stop for visitors interested in Shinto history without the crowds of Nagoya's larger shrines.
access: Meitetsu Tsushima Line from Nagoya, about 25 to 30 minutes, then roughly a 15-minute walk from Tsushima Station.

title: Takeshima Island
summary: A tiny forested island reachable only by a causeway that runs straight beneath a stone torii, said to bring good luck to couples who cross it together.
description:
Takeshima is a small, densely wooded island just off the coast of Gamagori, connected to the mainland by a roughly 387-meter causeway that crosses shallow, calm water. Its rocky outcrops, formed thousands of years ago and rising over 20 meters at their highest points, support an unusually dense and varied plant community for such a small area, over two hundred species by some counts, a diversity significant enough to earn the island National Natural Monument status in 1930.

The island's most distinctive feature is architectural rather than natural: the causeway passes directly beneath a large stone torii gate, one of the only places in Japan where a bridge runs straight through a shrine gateway rather than approaching it from the side. Local tradition holds that couples who cross the causeway together, passing under the torii, will be blessed with good fortune, and the walk is popular for that reason alone. At the island's center sits Yaotomi Shrine, said to date back to 1181 and dedicated to Benzaiten, one of the seven deities of good fortune associated with easy childbirth and marriage.

The short causeway walk and modest island loop make Takeshima an easy, low-effort stop for visitors continuing on to other parts of the Mikawa Bay coastline.
access: JR Tokaido Line from Nagoya to Gamagori Station, about 50 to 60 minutes, then a short walk to the causeway.

title: Toyokawa Inari
summary: A Zen Buddhist temple, not a shrine, whose grounds are nonetheless packed with roughly a thousand stone foxes, making it one of Japan's three great Inari pilgrimage sites.
description:
Despite its name and its thousand-plus fox statues, a symbol most visitors associate with Shinto Inari shrines, Toyokawa Inari is technically a Soto Zen Buddhist temple, formally named Myogon-ji, whose guardian deity happens to be a fox-riding form of the bodhisattva Dakiniten. That overlap between Buddhist and folk-Shinto imagery makes it genuinely distinctive among Japan's major Inari worship sites, and it is counted, alongside Kyoto's Fushimi Inari and Saga's Yutoku Inari, among the country's three great Inari pilgrimage destinations.

The temple's extensive grounds are lined with row after row of stone fox statues of every size, many donated by worshippers over generations seeking success in business, a common association with Inari devotion. A long approach lined with shops selling inari-zushi, the fried tofu pocket sushi named for the same fox connection, leads up to the main hall, giving the visit a genuine pilgrimage-town atmosphere rather than a single isolated building.

Being further from Nagoya than most of the region's other day-trip destinations, Toyokawa Inari sees fewer casual tourists and more dedicated worshippers, which gives it a noticeably different, more devotional atmosphere than the city's central shrines.
access: Meitetsu Toyokawa Line from Nagoya, about 70 to 80 minutes with a transfer, or JR to Toyokawa Station.

title: Shippo Art Village
summary: A craft village built around the revived Edo-era art of cloisonne enamel, in a town whose very name literally means 'cloisonne.'
description:
Shippo-yaki, the Japanese term for cloisonne enamelware, uses a colorful glass glaze fired onto a metal base and takes its name from a Buddhist term for the 'seven treasures,' a nod to the technique's jewel-like finish. Though cloisonne existed in Japan earlier, the craft's modern revival is generally traced to 1833, when a goldsmith named Tsunekichi Kaji, working in the Owari domain, became fascinated by imported Dutch cloisonne plates and reverse-engineered the technique through careful study, establishing this stretch of Owari as the country's production base for the craft.

The town where this happened became known simply as Shippo-cho, and it eventually merged into the modern city of Ama in 2010, though the name and craft tradition remain closely tied to the area. The Shippo Art Village opened in 2004 to promote the craft, which received formal designation as a traditional national craft in 1995, offering exhibition space alongside shops where visitors can buy contemporary cloisonne jewelry, dishware and decorative pieces made using techniques that trace directly back to Kaji's nineteenth-century experiments.

The village is a modest, single-purpose stop best suited to visitors with a specific interest in traditional crafts rather than a broader sightseeing itinerary.
access: Meitetsu Tsushima Line to Shippo Station, then about a 25-minute walk (or taxi from Kida Station), or Meitetsu bus to the Anmatsu stop, then about a 15-minute walk; roughly 40 to 50 minutes total from central Nagoya.

title: Ghibli Park
summary: A theme park built inside an existing public park rather than replacing it, folding Studio Ghibli's film worlds into real forest instead of building flat facades.
description:
Ghibli Park opened its first sections on November 1, 2022, built not from scratch but woven into the existing grounds of Expo 2005 Aichi Commemorative Park, also known as Moricoro Park, the site of the 2005 World Expo. That decision shapes the entire experience: rather than a conventional theme park with rides queued behind gates, Ghibli Park spreads its five themed areas across genuine forest and open parkland, opened in phases through 2022, 2023 and 2024.

Dondoko Forest, one of the first areas to open, centers on Satsuki and Mei's House from My Neighbor Totoro, tucked into real greenery with walking paths leading up a hillside to a large Totoro-shaped play structure. Ghibli's Grand Warehouse and Hill of Youth followed as part of the same initial phase, with Mononoke Village arriving in November 2023 and the Valley of Witches, inspired by Kiki's Delivery Service, completing the park's five areas in March 2024.

Because the park sits within a much larger public park, and because most areas require timed tickets booked well in advance, visitors should plan their entry slots before arriving rather than expecting walk-up access.
access: Higashiyama subway line from Nagoya Station to Fujigaoka Station (about 28 minutes), then transfer to the Linimo line to Ai-Chikyuhaku-Kinen-Koen Station (about 13 minutes); roughly 45 to 50 minutes total from central Nagoya including the transfer.

title: Moricoro Park (Expo 2005 Commemorative Park)
summary: The vast public park left behind by the 2005 World Expo, sharing its forests and lawns with Ghibli Park while still offering wide, free, un-ticketed grounds for a picnic or a bike ride.
description:
Long before Ghibli Park arrived, this site hosted the 2005 World Expo, and much of the infrastructure built for that event, wide lawns, wooded paths, ponds and a large Ferris wheel, was deliberately preserved afterward as a permanent public park rather than demolished. That history means Moricoro Park is considerably bigger than the ticketed Ghibli Park sections tucked inside it, and the large majority of its grounds remain completely free to enter and explore.

For visitors not interested in, or unable to book, Ghibli Park's timed tickets, Moricoro Park still offers a genuinely pleasant day out: seasonal flower fields that shift through the year, shaded cycling and walking paths, open lawns for picnics, and the original Expo-era Ferris wheel still turning for a modest fee. Families with young children in particular can spend a full day here without ever purchasing a Ghibli Park ticket, treating the anime-themed areas as an optional add-on rather than the whole point of the visit.

Because Ghibli Park's most Instagram-famous corners sit inside this larger free park, even a non-ticketed visit offers glimpses of the surrounding landscaping and atmosphere that made the site attractive to Studio Ghibli in the first place.
access: Higashiyama subway line from Nagoya Station to Fujigaoka Station (about 28 minutes), then transfer to the Linimo line to Ai-Chikyuhaku-Kinen-Koen Station (about 13 minutes); roughly 45 to 50 minutes total from central Nagoya including the transfer.

title: Masumida Shrine
summary: The 'first shrine' of old Owari Province, whose enshrined deity is said to have blessed the textile trade that turned this town into one of Japan's biggest fabric-producing cities.
description:
Masumida Shrine was founded well over 1,400 years ago and held the rank of ichinomiya, or 'first shrine,' of Owari Province, the highest-ranked shrine in the old provincial hierarchy, dedicated to the deity Amenoho-no-Akari-no-Mikoto, described in tradition as a grandson of the sun goddess Amaterasu and the elder brother of Ninigi-no-Mikoto, the deity from whom the imperial line is said to descend. The town that grew up around the shrine took its name directly from that rank, becoming Ichinomiya, and it developed through the Edo period into an important transport hub along the old Gifu highway.

The city's textile industry has roots reaching back to the Heian period, when the area became known for silk and striped cotton weaving, before expanding dramatically from the Meiji era into a major center of woolen textile production that continues, in a smaller form, today. Local tradition draws a direct line between the shrine and that industry, since the mother of the shrine's enshrined deity is associated with the god of textiles, giving the city's manufacturing history a genuinely local mythological explanation rather than a purely economic one.

The shrine grounds themselves are calm and largely local in character, visited far more by Ichinomiya residents than outside tourists, which makes them a good stop for visitors curious about how a specific Shinto shrine can shape an entire city's economic identity.
access: JR Tokaido Line or Meitetsu line from Nagoya to Owari-Ichinomiya Station, about 15 to 20 minutes, then a short walk.

title: Toyota Automobile Museum
summary: Not to be confused with Toyota's industrial-history museum near Nagoya Station, this is a broader, more international collection spanning the entire history of the automobile.
description:
Opened in April 1989 to mark Toyota Motor Corporation's fiftieth anniversary, the Toyota Automobile Museum takes a deliberately wider view than its name might suggest, covering the global history of the automobile from the earliest gasoline-powered cars of the late 1800s through to modern electric vehicles, rather than focusing narrowly on Toyota's own product line. Spread across a 46,700-square-meter site, the museum's Automobile Gallery displays over a hundred roadworthy vehicles, including genuinely rare pieces like a 1922 Grand Prix Sunbeam alongside classic American, European and Japanese models.

A separate Cultural Gallery pairs the vehicles themselves with roughly four thousand related cultural artifacts, vintage advertisements, toys, design sketches and other material that situates the cars within the broader design and consumer history of their eras. The museum's research collection runs even deeper, holding around two hundred thousand reference items including books, magazines and manufacturer catalogs, a resource used by researchers as much as casual visitors.

Since it sits in Nagakute, close to Ghibli Park and the Aichi Prefectural Ceramic Museum's general area, car enthusiasts visiting for Ghibli Park can reasonably combine both stops in a single day.
access: Higashiyama subway line from Nagoya Station to Fujigaoka Station, then the Linimo maglev line to Geidai-dori Station, about 40 minutes total from central Nagoya, followed by a roughly 5-minute walk to the museum.

title: Korankei Gorge
summary: A maple gorge planted nearly four centuries ago by a Zen abbot, now ranked among Japan's finest autumn-color valleys, with a red bridge as its signature shot.
description:
Korankei sits along the Tomoe River, a tributary of the Yahagi River, in the Asuke area of Toyota City, a valley whose reputation for autumn color is tied directly to a specific historical decision. According to local tradition, many of the roughly three thousand maple trees that now fill the gorge, spanning eleven different varieties, were planted starting in 1634 by the eleventh abbot of Kojaku-ji, a Zen temple founded in 1427 that still stands nearby, who deliberately set out to beautify the valley and encouraged later visitors to add more trees of their own.

That centuries-long planting effort has produced one of the settings regularly cited among Japan's finest autumn foliage destinations, with a network of paths leading through a tunnel of maples toward Taigetsukyo, a red arched bridge that has become the valley's most photographed single spot. Nearby stands Goshiki-Momiji, a single large maple tree notable for displaying five different leaf colors simultaneously as the season progresses. During peak autumn weeks the gorge is illuminated after dark for evening viewing, extending visiting hours well past sunset.

Outside the main autumn season the gorge is a quieter, simply pleasant river valley for walking, though its reputation and crowds are overwhelmingly tied to the few weeks of peak color each November.
access: Meitetsu train to Toyotoshi Station, then a bus to Asuke, roughly 100-120 minutes total from central Nagoya (longer during the November autumn-color season due to traffic).

title: Odori Park
summary: A twelve-block green spine through downtown Sapporo that turns into a snow-sculpture fairground every February and a beer garden every summer.
description:
Odori Park is less a single park than a long civic stage that changes costume with the seasons. Locals cut through it on the way to work, sit on its benches with a convenience-store coffee at lunch, and pack it shoulder to shoulder for the Sapporo Snow Festival in February, when massive ice and snow sculptures line the walkways for about ten days. In summer the same lawns host a six-week beer garden where several breweries set up tents side by side, and in autumn the ginkgo and elm trees along the park turn a deep gold.

The park stretches between Odori Station, which several subway lines pass through, and is a short walk from JR Sapporo Station, so it works well as a orientation point for a first day in the city. The Sapporo TV Tower at its eastern end and the clock tower a block away are both easy add-ons to a stroll through.

During the Snow Festival the crowds are heaviest in the evening when the sculptures are lit up, so visiting in the mid-morning gives a calmer look at the same artwork with shorter lines for food stalls. Outside festival season, the park is at its quietest on weekday mornings before the lunch crowd arrives. Because Hokkaido's climate swings hard between seasons, check ahead if a specific event is the reason for the visit, since snow and beer-garden dates shift slightly from year to year.
access: Runs through central Sapporo between Odori Station (Namboku, Toho and Tozai subway lines) and JR Sapporo Station, roughly a 10-minute walk to the north end.
address: Odori Nishi 1-12 chome, Chuo-ku, Sapporo, Hokkaido

title: Sapporo TV Tower
summary: The red steel tower bookending Odori Park, offering a straight-down view of the snow sculptures or beer tents depending on the month.
description:
Built in 1957 at the eastern tip of Odori Park, this red lattice tower is one of Sapporo's most recognizable silhouettes even though, at roughly 90 meters, it is modest compared to observation towers in bigger cities. Its main draw is the angle: because it sits right at the end of the park, the observation deck gives a straight, elevated view down the length of Odori and out toward the mountains ringing the city, including Mount Moiwa on a clear day.

The deck is small enough that a visit rarely takes more than 30-45 minutes, which makes it an easy stop before or after a walk through the park rather than a destination in itself. At night, the tower itself is lit up and photographs well from the park below, which is part of why it appears in so many Sapporo postcards.

Because it sits directly above one of the park's subway exits, it can get a burst of visitors right after tour buses unload; going up in the first hour after opening or later in the evening tends to be calmer. During the Snow Festival the deck offers a bird's-eye view of the sculptures below, which is worth the ticket price in winter specifically, while in other seasons the view is pleasant but less dramatic.
access: At the east end of Odori Park, directly above the Odori Station subway exits.
