title: Kanawa Floating Oyster Restaurant
summary: A restaurant built inside a moored boat on the Motoyasu River, serving multi-course oyster meals a short walk from the Atomic Bomb Dome.
description:
Hiroshima Prefecture is one of Japan's largest producers of farmed oysters, and the calm, nutrient-rich waters of the Seto Inland Sea around Hiroshima Bay have supported oyster cultivation for centuries. Kanawa takes that local specialty and serves it aboard a converted boat permanently moored on the Motoyasu River, within easy walking distance of Peace Memorial Park, giving diners a dedicated setting built entirely around the ingredient.

The restaurant offers set courses that typically move through several preparations of oyster in one sitting, such as raw, grilled, fried, and simmered in a hot pot, letting first-time visitors sample the range of textures and flavors a single ingredient can take on rather than committing to just one style. Seasonal availability affects the menu, since Japanese oysters are generally at their best from autumn through early spring.

Because it operates from a boat with limited seating, reservations are strongly recommended, particularly for dinner or during peak oyster season, and the combination of a distinctive setting with a genuinely well-regarded kitchen has made it a long-standing favorite among Hiroshima diners rather than a purely tourist-oriented novelty.
access: 10-minute walk from Hiroshima Station, or 5-minute walk from Kamiyacho-nishi tram stop; moored on the Motoyasu River near Heiwa Ohashi bridge.
address: Ote-machi, Naka Ward, Hiroshima, Hiroshima Prefecture

title: Hiroshima Flower Festival
summary: A large early-May street festival along Peace Boulevard, built around parades and stage performances rather than flower displays alone, and timed to Golden Week.
description:
The Hiroshima Flower Festival began in 1977, launched partly as a way to give the city a positive, forward-looking public event during the Golden Week holiday period, following decades of postwar recovery. It is held annually across three days in early May along Heiwa Odori, or Peace Boulevard, the wide central avenue that runs near Peace Memorial Park, and regularly draws very large crowds, making it one of the biggest annual events in the city.

Despite the name, the festival is less a garden show and more a citywide street festival, featuring parades with floats and marching bands, stage performances of traditional and contemporary music and dance, food stalls lining the boulevard, and flower displays and decorations woven throughout the route. Local schools, community groups, and businesses all take part, giving it a strong grassroots, city-wide character rather than a purely tourist-facing event.

Because it falls during Golden Week, one of Japan's busiest domestic travel periods, accommodation in central Hiroshima can book up well in advance for festival dates, and the crowds along Peace Boulevard can be substantial, so visitors planning around it should expect a lively, dense atmosphere rather than a quiet stroll.
access: Centered on Heiwa Odori (Peace Boulevard); reachable on foot from Hiroshima Station or Kamiyacho tram stops.
address: Heiwa Odori (Peace Boulevard), Naka Ward, Hiroshima, Hiroshima Prefecture

title: Itsukushima Shrine
summary: A vermillion shrine complex built on stilts over the tidal flats of Miyajima, designed so its halls and famous offshore gate appear to float at high tide.
description:
Itsukushima Shrine's current layout dates largely to the 12th century, when powerful warlord Taira no Kiyomori rebuilt and expanded an earlier shrine on the site into the elaborate complex of pier-supported halls, corridors, and stages seen today. Because the entire island of Miyajima was traditionally considered sacred, the shrine's founders built out over the water rather than on the land itself, and the structure was engineered to allow tides to flow beneath the buildings without damaging them.

At high tide, the shrine's connected halls and the offshore torii gate appear to float on the sea, while at low tide visitors can walk out across the exposed sand to the base of the gate itself, giving the site two quite different visual characters depending on when it is visited. The complex includes a noh stage still used for performances, a treasure hall, and long connecting corridors, and it was jointly registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 along with its setting on Miyajima.

Because tide timing significantly changes the experience and photos, it is worth checking tide tables in advance; many visitors try to see the shrine at both high and low tide if their schedule allows, often by staying overnight on the island.
access: 10-minute ferry from Miyajimaguchi Station to Miyajima pier, then about a 10-minute walk to the shrine; Miyajimaguchi is roughly 30 minutes from central Hiroshima by JR train or tram plus ferry.

title: Great Torii of Miyajima
summary: The vermillion gate standing offshore from Itsukushima Shrine, one of Japan's most photographed landmarks and one that visitors can walk right up to at low tide.
description:
The torii marking the sea approach to Itsukushima Shrine has stood in some form since at least the 12th century, though the current gate dates to 1875 and is built mainly of camphor wood, chosen partly for its resistance to rot and marine pests. Unlike many torii gates, it is not fixed into the seabed with deep foundations; instead its considerable weight, reinforced with stones packed into the upper crossbeam, holds it upright against tides and typhoons.

The gate's appearance changes dramatically with the tide: at high tide it appears to rise directly from the sea, reinforcing the impression of the shrine complex floating nearby, while at low tide the surrounding sand flats are exposed and visitors can walk out across the seabed to stand at its base. The gate underwent a major restoration completed in 2022 after several years of scaffolding, its first large-scale renovation in roughly three decades.

Evening illumination after sunset is another distinct viewing window, when the gate and shrine are lit against the dark water, drawing a different crowd than the daytime low-tide walk. Because of the gate's fame, the immediate viewing area along the shore can be crowded, especially around sunset and low tide windows in peak season.
access: 10-minute ferry from Miyajimaguchi Station to Miyajima pier, then about a 10-minute walk along the waterfront.
address: Offshore from Itsukushima Shrine, Miyajima-cho, Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima Prefecture

title: Mount Misen Ropeway
summary: A two-stage cable car up Miyajima's sacred mountain, cutting a roughly two-hour hike down to about fifteen minutes and ending at an observatory with views across the Seto Inland Sea.
description:
Mount Misen is the highest point on Miyajima and has been treated as sacred ground for centuries, associated with the Buddhist monk Kobo Daishi, who is said to have practiced ascetic training on the mountain in the early 9th century. A small hall near the summit contains a flame traditionally said to have burned continuously since his time, and it is sometimes described as one of the sources used to light the Flame of Peace in Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Park.

The ropeway climbs the mountain in two connected stages from a lower station reached by bus or a walk from the ferry pier, cutting what would otherwise be a hike of roughly two hours each way down to about a fifteen-minute ride. From the upper ropeway station, it is still a further walk of around 20 to 30 minutes over uneven trail to reach the actual summit and its observation deck, which looks out over the forested island, the Great Torii far below, and the wider Seto Inland Sea toward Honshu.

The forest along the ropeway route and summit trail is part of a protected natural area and is home to wild macaques and deer, and the whole mountain is a well-known spot for autumn foliage, typically peaking in mid-to-late November.
access: About 15 minutes on foot or a short bus ride from Miyajima pier to the Momijidani ropeway station, then a two-stage cable car ride of roughly 15 minutes to the upper station.
address: Momijidani Park, Miyajima-cho, Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima Prefecture

title: Miyajima Omotesando Shopping Street
summary: The main approach street between Miyajima's ferry pier and Itsukushima Shrine, lined with souvenir shops, oyster stalls, and the wooden rice paddle Miyajima is known for.
description:
Omotesando runs for a few hundred meters between the ferry pier and the approach to Itsukushima Shrine, and it has served as the island's commercial main street for generations, adapting over time from a fishing and pilgrim town's shopping row into today's mix of souvenir shops, food stalls, and craft workshops. It remains largely pedestrian and is one of the few parts of the island with a dense concentration of shops, since most of Miyajima outside this strip is residential, forested, or shrine grounds.

Among its specialties, the street is closely associated with the shamoji, a wooden rice paddle said to have originated on Miyajima in the late 18th century, now sold in every size from kitchen tool to oversized decorative pieces. Food stalls along the street sell grilled and fried oysters, another Hiroshima specialty, as well as the maple-leaf-shaped cakes called momiji manju, often available freshly made and warm.

Because the street funnels essentially all foot traffic between the ferry and the shrine, it can get crowded during midday hours in peak season, and wild deer, which roam freely across the island, are a regular presence looking for food scraps or occasionally nosing at paper bags.
access: Directly connects Miyajima ferry pier to the approach of Itsukushima Shrine, about a 10-minute walk end to end.

title: Momiji Manju Workshops, Miyajima
summary: Small bakeries along Miyajima's main street where visitors can watch maple-leaf-shaped cakes cast and filled in individual molds before buying them warm.
description:
Momiji manju are small, maple-leaf-shaped cakes with a sponge-cake-like exterior wrapped around a filling, most traditionally sweet red bean paste, though modern shops offer variations such as custard, chocolate, or cheese. The confection is generally traced to Miyajima in the early 20th century, and the maple leaf shape references the island's Momijidani, or "Maple Valley," known for its autumn foliage, though the cakes themselves are sold and eaten year-round.

Several bakeries along Omotesando and the surrounding streets make the cakes on-site using individual cast-iron molds, and it is common to see the process happening in the shop window: batter poured into open molds, filling added, then the molds closed and flipped to cook each cake individually on a rotating rig. Buying a cake straight off this line, still warm, is a noticeably different experience from the packaged versions sold as souvenirs elsewhere in Japan.

A related, more recent variation is fried momiji manju, dipped in batter and deep-fried to order, which has become its own minor specialty on the island and is often sold from separate stalls or counters near the main shops.
access: Along Miyajima Omotesando shopping street, a short walk from the ferry pier.

title: Daisho-in Temple
summary: A hillside Shingon Buddhist temple on Miyajima with a dense mix of statues, carved stairways, and Tibetan-style prayer wheels, offering a quieter counterpart to Itsukushima Shrine.
description:
Daisho-in is traditionally considered one of the oldest and most important temples on Miyajima, associated with the same Kobo Daishi tradition tied to Mount Misen, and it once served as a temple of significant standing within Japanese Shingon Buddhism. It sits at the base of Mount Misen, a short uphill walk from Itsukushima Shrine, and unlike the shrine's open, waterborne layout, Daisho-in's grounds are dense and layered, built up the hillside with stairways, halls, and garden paths.

One of its most recognizable features is a stone stairway lined with metal prayer wheels inscribed with sutras, which visitors can spin by hand while climbing, said to confer the same merit as reading the text inside. The temple grounds also include a cave hall containing statues representing the 88 temples of the Shikoku pilgrimage, letting visitors symbolically complete that famous pilgrimage route in miniature within a single building, along with numerous smaller Jizo statues, some dressed in knitted caps left by visitors.

Because it draws far fewer visitors than Itsukushima Shrine despite being only a short walk away, Daisho-in tends to be a noticeably calmer stop, and its varied, close-quarters layout rewards slower exploration rather than a quick pass-through.
access: About a 15-minute walk from Miyajima pier, near the base of the Mount Misen ropeway route.

title: Miyajima Aquarium
summary: A mid-sized aquarium on Miyajima focused on marine life of the Seto Inland Sea, including a regularly performed sea lion and seal show.
description:
Miyajima Aquarium, sometimes called Miyajima Public Aquarium, was substantially rebuilt and reopened in 2011 after decades operating in an older facility on roughly the same site, and it focuses heavily on species found in the surrounding Seto Inland Sea rather than exotic or deep-ocean animals from elsewhere. Tanks are organized loosely by habitat, moving from the shallow tidal flats around Miyajima itself through to open water species, giving the collection a fairly coherent regional identity.

Among its residents are finless porpoises, native to the Seto Inland Sea and rarely displayed at other Japanese aquariums, along with sea otters, seals, and sea lions that perform in a scheduled outdoor show through the day. A penguin enclosure and various smaller tanks of local fish and invertebrates round out the collection, and the facility is sized to be manageable in an hour or two, making it a reasonable add-on rather than a full-day destination.

Given that most of Miyajima's other attractions are shrines, temples, and hiking routes, the aquarium is a useful option for families traveling with younger children who may need a change of pace partway through a day on the island.
access: About a 20-minute walk from Miyajima pier along the coast, or a short taxi ride; also reachable by local bus.

title: Five-Story Pagoda, Miyajima
summary: A 15th-century pagoda on a hillside above Itsukushima Shrine, one of the island's most photographed structures thanks to its elevated view over the shrine and torii below.
description:
The five-story pagoda standing above Itsukushima Shrine dates to 1407 and blends Japanese and Chinese-influenced architectural styles typical of the Muromachi period, with vermillion coloring that echoes the shrine complex below despite being administratively separate from it. It stands roughly 27 meters tall on a small rise near Toyokuni Shrine, and while its interior is not generally open to the public, the exterior and its surrounding grounds are freely accessible.

What makes the pagoda a particularly popular photo stop is its elevated position relative to the shrine and the Great Torii, allowing views that combine the pagoda's own tiered roofline with the shrine complex, the gate, and the sea beyond in a single frame, especially from certain angles along the path leading up to it. This makes it one of the more reliably photogenic spots on the island beyond the shrine and gate themselves.

The pagoda sits immediately next to Senjokaku, the large open pavilion also known as the Hall of a Thousand Mats, and the two are typically visited together as part of the same short uphill walk from the shrine's main approach.
access: About a 5-minute walk uphill from Itsukushima Shrine's exit, near Senjokaku.

title: Senjokaku (Toyokuni Shrine)
summary: A vast open wooden pavilion on Miyajima commissioned in 1587 and left unfinished, still lacking walls, ceiling panels, and its front doors more than four centuries later.
description:
Senjokaku, whose name translates roughly to "Pavilion of a Thousand Mats," was commissioned in 1587 by warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi as a hall for chanting Buddhist sutras on behalf of fallen soldiers. Hideyoshi died in 1598 before construction was completed, and the building was simply left as it was, without ceiling boards over parts of the structure, front doors, and other finishing details, giving it an unusually raw, exposed timber-frame appearance compared with most Japanese religious buildings.

The hall now functions as Toyokuni Shrine, and despite its unfinished state it is enormous by the standards of traditional Japanese wooden architecture, supported by large pillars and open on most sides to the surrounding air, which keeps it naturally cool and breezy even in summer. Visitors can walk across its wide wooden floor, and numerous large votive paintings and plaques donated over the centuries hang from its exposed beams and walls.

It stands immediately beside the five-story pagoda on the hillside above Itsukushima Shrine, and the two are commonly visited as a pair on the short uphill detour from the shrine's exit.
access: About a 5-minute walk uphill from Itsukushima Shrine's exit, adjacent to the five-story pagoda.

title: Momijidani Park
summary: A wooded valley park at the base of Mount Misen whose name means 'maple valley,' widely regarded as Miyajima's best spot for autumn foliage.
description:
Momijidani Park sits at the foot of Mount Misen, a short walk inland from Itsukushima Shrine, and takes its name directly from the maple trees planted throughout the valley, many of which are estimated to be well over a century old. A stream runs through the park crossed by several small bridges, and wild deer wander freely across its lawns and paths, generally undisturbed by visitors and reasonably comfortable being photographed at a respectful distance.

The park is most crowded, and arguably most striking, during autumn foliage season, typically peaking in mid-to-late November, when the maple canopy turns deep red and orange and draws large numbers of both domestic and international visitors. Outside that window it remains a pleasant, shaded rest stop, particularly useful in summer given the relative lack of shade around the shrine and torii areas closer to the water.

The lower station of the Mount Misen ropeway sits at the edge of the park, so many visitors pass through Momijidani anyway on their way up the mountain, making it easy to combine with a ropeway trip rather than requiring a separate detour.
access: About a 15-minute walk from Miyajima pier, or a short bus ride toward the ropeway station.

title: Senkoji Temple
summary: A vermillion hillside temple above Onomichi, founded over a thousand years ago and now a fixed reference point in views across the city's rooftops to the Seto Inland Sea.
description:
Senkoji is said to have been founded in 806, and its bright vermillion halls sit partway up the hillside that rises directly behind Onomichi's harbor-front streets, making the temple visible from much of the lower town and, in turn, giving temple visitors sweeping views back down over the city's tiled roofs to the strait and islands beyond. The temple complex includes several halls and a scattering of large, naturally weathered boulders integrated into the grounds, some inscribed or associated with local legend.

Onomichi is sometimes described as a city of temples, with more than two dozen Buddhist temples spread across its hillside neighborhoods, and Senkoji functions as the anchor point of the popular Onomichi Temple Walk, a signposted walking route that links many of them along narrow stone stairways and alleys. Senkoji itself, along with the adjoining Senkoji Park, tends to be the most visited stop on that route given its striking hilltop position and easy access via the Onomichi Ropeway.

The surrounding hillside is also known for cherry blossoms in spring, and the combination of temple, boulders, and layered city-and-sea views makes it one of the more consistently photographed spots in Onomichi.
access: Reachable by the Onomichi Ropeway from Nagaeguchi Station near JR Onomichi Station, or via a signposted walking path up the hillside; about 90 minutes to 2 hours from central Hiroshima by JR train.

title: Onomichi Ropeway
summary: A short cable car connecting the base of Onomichi's hillside temple district to Senkoji Park at the top, replacing what would otherwise be a steep uphill walk.
description:
The ropeway climbs the hill behind central Onomichi from a lower station near Nagaeguchi, just a few minutes from JR Onomichi Station, up to Senkoji Park at the summit in a ride of only a few minutes. It has operated in some form since the 1950s, built specifically to give easier access to Senkoji Temple and the panoramic viewpoint above it without requiring visitors to climb the hillside's many stone stairways on foot.

From the upper station, a short walk leads to the main observation deck at Senkoji Park, which looks out over Onomichi's dense, tightly packed rooftops, the narrow strait separating Honshu from Mukaishima, and the wider Seto Inland Sea dotted with small islands and passing ferries. The view is considered one of the better easily accessible cityscape-and-sea views in the Setouchi region, and it is popular at both midday and sunset.

Many visitors ride the ropeway up and then walk back down through the temple district on foot, following the Onomichi Temple Walk route past Senkoji and several other temples, alleys, and the Path of Literature lined with stone monuments inscribed with lines from writers connected to the city.
access: Lower station a short walk from JR Onomichi Station via Nagaeguchi; ride takes about 3 minutes to the upper station at Senkoji Park.

title: Onomichi Hondori Shopping Street
summary: A roughly 1.6-kilometer covered arcade running the length of Onomichi's old port town, mixing retro shopfronts, secondhand bookstores, and casual eateries.
description:
Hondori runs in a long, mostly straight line parallel to the waterfront through the older part of Onomichi, and much of it is covered, giving it a slightly faded, retro character shaped by the port town's history as a shipping and trade hub going back to the medieval period. The arcade mixes still-operating traditional shops selling local goods with a fair number of vacant or converted storefronts, a visible sign of the town's shrinking population that has also made it attractive to independent cafes, secondhand bookstores, and small galleries moving into low-rent space.

Onomichi has a literary reputation in Japan, having been the setting or home for several well-known writers and filmmakers, and Hondori and its side alleys retain something of that atmosphere, with narrow lanes branching uphill toward the temple district and its many stone stairways. The street is a natural base for exploring the town on foot, since it connects easily to both the harbor and the lower stations of the Onomichi Temple Walk and Neko no Hosomichi cat alley.

Casual food options along the street include Onomichi's distinctive style of ramen, as well as smaller cafes serving coffee and simple lunch sets, making it easy to combine shopping with a meal break.
access: Runs parallel to the waterfront a short walk from JR Onomichi Station.

title: Senkoji Park
summary: The hilltop park surrounding Senkoji Temple, home to Onomichi's main citywide observation deck and one of the region's better-regarded cherry blossom spots.
description:
Senkoji Park occupies the summit area around Senkoji Temple, reached either via the Onomichi Ropeway or a walking trail up through the temple district below. Its main draw is the observation platform, which looks out across Onomichi's densely packed rooftops, the narrow Onomichi Strait separating the mainland from Mukaishima island, and the wider Seto Inland Sea beyond, with the various bridges of the Shimanami Kaido sometimes visible in clear weather.

The park is planted with a large number of cherry trees and has long been recognized as one of Japan's notable cherry blossom viewing spots, drawing crowds in early April when the trees bloom against the backdrop of the temple's vermillion halls and the sea view below. Large, naturally weathered rock formations are scattered through the grounds, some associated with local folklore, adding texture to what is otherwise a fairly compact hilltop park.

Because the park sits directly around Senkoji Temple, most visitors treat the two as a single stop, and the walking paths down from the park connect into the broader Onomichi Temple Walk route through the hillside's other temples and narrow lanes.
access: Reachable via the Onomichi Ropeway from Nagaeguchi, or on foot up the hillside stairways from central Onomichi.

title: Neko no Hosomichi (Cat Alley)
summary: A narrow, roughly 1-kilometer stone path winding through Onomichi's hillside neighborhoods, decorated over the years with small painted stones and folk-art touches inspired by the area's resident cats.
description:
Neko no Hosomichi, literally "Cat's Narrow Path," runs along part of the hillside route between the town center and the temple district above, threading between old wooden houses, retaining walls, and stairways in one of Onomichi's older residential neighborhoods. Like much of the town's hillside, it developed as housing squeezed onto steep terrain overlooking the harbor, and the resulting maze of narrow lanes has become part of the area's appeal for visitors exploring on foot.

The path takes its name from the number of cats that have long lived in the neighborhood, and over time local artists and residents added small hand-painted stones with cat designs along the route, alongside a scattering of cat-themed folk art, murals, and a small private gallery dedicated to local artist Shodo Kubota's cat-and-stone artwork. The actual number of cats encountered on any given walk varies and is not something the area guarantees, since they are free-roaming rather than kept as a formal attraction.

Because the lane connects into the wider network of hillside alleys and stairways near Senkoji, it works well as part of a longer walk through Onomichi's temple district rather than a single isolated stop, and the slower pace of wandering its turns is arguably more the point than reaching any specific endpoint.
access: Accessible from the hillside paths near Senkoji Temple and the Path of Literature, a short walk up from central Onomichi.
address: Higashitsuchido-cho / Nagaecho area, Onomichi, Hiroshima Prefecture

title: Onomichi Ramen
summary: A regional ramen style built on a soy-sauce broth enriched with rendered pork back fat, developed in this Setouchi port town and now considered one of Japan's notable local ramen varieties.
description:
Onomichi ramen is generally traced back to noodle stalls that began operating in the town in the years following the Second World War, and it has since become recognized alongside a handful of other regional styles, such as Hakata and Kitakata ramen, as one of Japan's distinct local ramen traditions. Its defining feature is a clear soy-sauce-based broth typically made from chicken or pork bones and dried small fish, into which small chunks of rendered pork back fat are mixed, giving the soup a lightly rich, slightly sweet character despite its relatively clear appearance.

The noodles used are typically flat and slightly wide rather than the thin curly noodles associated with some other regional styles, and toppings tend to be kept fairly simple, commonly sliced chashu pork, bamboo shoots, green onion, and a piece of narutomaki fish cake. A number of long-running, family-run shops around Hondori and the harbor area are considered among the originators of the style, though as with most regional food traditions, opinions on the single best shop vary widely among locals.

Because Onomichi is a compact town, most of its well-regarded ramen shops sit within easy walking distance of JR Onomichi Station and the main Hondori shopping street, making it simple to combine a bowl with sightseeing in the temple district.
access: Numerous shops within walking distance of JR Onomichi Station and along the Hondori shopping street.

title: Shimanami Kaido Cycling Route
summary: A roughly 70-kilometer cycling route across a chain of bridges linking Onomichi in Hiroshima Prefecture to Imabari in Shikoku, widely regarded as one of Japan's best long-distance rides.
description:
The Shimanami Kaido opened as a full expressway and cycling route in 1999, connecting Honshu to Shikoku by threading a chain of bridges across six small islands in the Seto Inland Sea: Mukaishima, Innoshima, Ikuchijima, Omishima, Hakatajima, and Oshima. Unlike most of Japan's other Honshu-Shikoku crossings, this route was built with a dedicated, largely separated cycling and walking path running alongside the motor traffic lanes across every bridge, which is a major reason it developed a strong international cycling reputation.

The full one-way ride from Onomichi to Imabari covers roughly 70 kilometers and can typically be completed in a single day by a reasonably fit rider, though many visitors break it into a more relaxed two-day trip, stopping at island towns, temples such as Kosanji, and rental cycle terminals along the way. Bicycle rental is widely available at terminals on both ends and at several points in between, including standard cross-frame bikes, road bikes, and e-bikes, with one-way rental allowing pickup on one end and drop-off on the other.

Route markings, rest stops, and toilets are placed at regular intervals, and the blue line painted along much of the path makes navigation straightforward even for first-time visitors unfamiliar with the islands.
access: Starts near JR Onomichi Station in Hiroshima Prefecture and ends near Imabari Station in Ehime Prefecture; Onomichi is about 90 minutes to 2 hours from central Hiroshima by JR train.

title: Kosanji Temple and Hill of Hope
summary: A privately built 20th-century temple on the Shimanami Kaido island of Ikuchijima, paired with a sprawling white Italian-marble sculpture garden completed only in 2000.
description:
Kosanji was built starting in 1936 by a local businessman as a memorial temple dedicated to his mother, and construction continued for more than three decades, with individual halls modeled after or inspired by famous temples and shrines elsewhere in Japan, including structures echoing Nikko's Yomeimon gate and Kyoto's Byodo-in. The result is less a single traditional temple than an assembled collection of replica and original halls, gates, and a museum of Buddhist art, all on one hillside site in the small town of Setoda.

Behind the temple, a separate and more recent addition called the Hill of Hope, or Miraishin no Oka, spreads across roughly 5,000 square meters of white marble sculpture and terracing, all carved from around 3,000 tonnes of Carrara marble imported from Italy. Designed and built over sixteen years by Hiroshima-born sculptor Kazuto Kuetani, the garden was opened to the public in 2000 and has no formal religious function, existing purely as a large-scale sculptural artwork with sweeping views over the town and the Seto Inland Sea from its highest terraces.

The combination of dense, colorful traditional-style temple halls followed by an almost entirely white, modern marble garden makes for a fairly unusual visit, and it has become one of the signature stops for cyclists and drivers passing through Setoda on the Shimanami Kaido.
access: About 5-minute walk from Setoda port on Ikuchijima island; roughly 1 to 1.5 hours from Onomichi by direct bus, or reachable via the Shimanami Kaido cycling route.

title: Innoshima Suigun Castle
summary: A small hilltop museum on Innoshima built in 1983 to house artifacts of the Murakami Suigun, the seafaring clan that controlled shipping through this stretch of the Seto Inland Sea for centuries.
description:
The Murakami Suigun were a maritime clan active in the Seto Inland Sea from roughly the 14th through 16th centuries, often described in English as pirates but functioning more as toll-collecting naval escorts and shipping guides who used their deep knowledge of the region's dangerous tidal currents to pilot vessels safely through the narrow straits between islands. Innoshima, one of the Shimanami Kaido's chain of islands, was one of the clan's main bases of operation, and some form of fortification is believed to have stood at this hilltop site historically.

The present castle-form building was constructed in 1983, not as a reconstruction of a specific historical structure but as a museum designed in castle style to display weapons, armor, documents, and other artifacts connected to the Murakami Suigun and their role in regional maritime history. Its turret houses a small exhibition space, and the surrounding hilltop grounds offer views over Innoshima's coastline and the bridges of the Shimanami Kaido nearby.

Because it is a modest, purpose-built museum rather than an original castle, it tends to appeal most to visitors specifically interested in the Murakami Suigun story or in Seto Inland Sea maritime history, and it makes a manageable stop for those cycling or driving the Shimanami Kaido through Innoshima.
access: About 15 minutes by taxi or local bus from Innoshima's ferry terminals; reachable via the Shimanami Kaido cycling and driving route.

title: Tatara Bridge
summary: A large cable-stayed bridge on the Shimanami Kaido that held the record for the world's longest cable-stayed span from its 1999 opening until 2008.
description:
Tatara Bridge connects Ikuchijima, on the Hiroshima Prefecture side of the Shimanami Kaido, to Omishima across the border in Ehime Prefecture, and it opened to traffic on May 1, 1999. Its central span measures 890 meters, and at the time of completion this made it the longest cable-stayed bridge span in the world, a title it held until being surpassed by China's Sutong Bridge in 2008; it remains one of the longest such spans anywhere.

The bridge's distinctive silhouette, with two tall white support towers and a wide fan of cables, has made it something of a visual signature for the Shimanami Kaido route as a whole, appearing in much of the promotional photography for the crossing. Like the other bridges along the route, it carries a dedicated cycling and walking lane separated from vehicle traffic, and crossing it on a bicycle, with open sea views on both sides and the cable towers rising directly overhead, is often cited by cyclists as one of the highlights of the full Shimanami Kaido ride.

A roadside park near the Ikuchijima end of the bridge offers a place to stop, rest, and photograph the structure from below without needing to cross it.
access: Reached via the Shimanami Kaido cycling route or expressway between Ikuchijima and Omishima islands.

title: Hirayama Ikuo Museum of Art
summary: A museum on Ikuchijima dedicated to painter Ikuo Hirayama, a survivor of the Hiroshima bombing whose Silk Road landscapes became some of postwar Japan's best-known Nihonga paintings.
description:
Ikuo Hirayama was born in 1930 in Setoda, the small port town on Ikuchijima where this museum now stands, and as a teenager he was exposed to radiation while working near Hiroshima at the time of the atomic bombing, an experience that shaped much of his later artistic and humanitarian work. He went on to become one of the most prominent Nihonga, or traditional Japanese-style painters, of the postwar era, known especially for large-scale works depicting Silk Road landscapes across Central Asia, the Middle East, and China, produced during decades of travel along that route.

Opened in 1997 in his hometown, the museum holds the largest collection of Hirayama's work, spanning childhood drawings that hint at early talent through to his mature Silk Road paintings, alongside sketches, travel diaries, and personal items documenting his career. Hirayama was also known for advocacy around cultural heritage preservation internationally, and some exhibits touch on that side of his work as well as his purely painted output.

Because the museum sits in Setoda alongside Kosanji Temple and the Hill of Hope, the two make a natural pairing for visitors passing through this stretch of the Shimanami Kaido on Ikuchijima.

access: Short walk from Setoda port on Ikuchijima island, near Kosanji Temple.

title: Yamato Museum (Kure Maritime Museum)
summary: A shipbuilding-city museum in Kure centered on a 26-meter scale model of the battleship Yamato, built at one-tenth scale by the same shipyard that constructed the original.
description:
Kure has been one of Japan's major naval shipbuilding centers since the late 19th century, when it was chosen as the site of an Imperial Japanese Navy arsenal, and that industrial history is the museum's central subject. Opened in 2005, the Yamato Museum takes its popular name from its most prominent exhibit, a roughly 26.3-meter-long, one-tenth scale model of the battleship Yamato, which was built and launched from Kure in 1940 and remains one of the largest battleships ever constructed.

Beyond the Yamato model, the museum's galleries cover the broader history of Kure as a shipbuilding city, from its naval arsenal origins through wartime shipbuilding and the city's postwar shift toward commercial shipbuilding and industry, using ship models, salvaged artifacts, and technical displays. Exhibits also address the human and civilian side of the city's wartime experience, including Kure's own bombing during the war, alongside the more technical shipbuilding content.

The museum sits directly across from the JMSDF Kure Museum, home to the decommissioned submarine Akishio, and the two are commonly visited together given their shared focus on Kure's naval and maritime history and their close proximity to each other near the harbor.
access: About 5-minute walk from JR Kure Station; Kure is roughly 30 to 40 minutes from central Hiroshima by JR train.

title: JMSDF Kure Museum (Iron Whale Museum)
summary: A free naval museum in Kure built around a real decommissioned submarine, the Akishio, which visitors can walk through interior compartments of.
description:
The JMSDF Kure Museum, widely known by its nickname "Iron Whale Museum," opened in 2007 to explain the history and work of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, with particular focus on submarine operations and coastal minesweeping, both closely tied to Kure's role as a naval base city. Its centerpiece is the Akishio, a Yushio-class diesel-electric submarine launched in 1985 and decommissioned in 2004, which was brought ashore and installed as a walk-through exhibit rather than simply displayed from the outside.

Visitors can walk through much of the submarine's original interior, including crew berths, the captain's quarters, and operational spaces, largely preserved as they were when the vessel was in active service, making it one of the only places in Japan where the public can enter a former Japanese navy submarine. Indoor galleries cover the JMSDF's postwar formation and its minesweeping work clearing wartime ordnance from Japanese waters, a lesser-known but significant part of the country's postwar reconstruction.

Admission is free, reflecting its status as a public defense-related facility rather than a private museum, and an on-site cafe serves a curry recipe based on the type served aboard JMSDF vessels. It sits directly across from the Yamato Museum, and the two are typically visited together.
access: About 5-minute walk from JR Kure Station, near the Yamato Museum; Kure is roughly 30 to 40 minutes from central Hiroshima by JR train.

title: Kure Warship Curry
summary: A style of curry rice served in Kure that follows recipes and formats based on those historically cooked aboard Japanese naval vessels, sold at restaurants across the city.
description:
Curry became a regular meal aboard Imperial Japanese Navy ships in part because it was practical to prepare in bulk and helped sailors keep track of days at sea, since it was traditionally served on a fixed day of the week, a practice the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force has continued into the present with each vessel often having its own house recipe. Because Kure has been a major naval base since the Meiji era and remains home to JMSDF facilities today, the city has leaned into this connection, branding a local style of curry rice as "Kaigun Curry," or navy curry, sold at restaurants across town.

Menus and exact recipes vary by restaurant, since many are modeled on the specific recipe of a particular current or former vessel, but the format is generally a thick, mild curry roux served over rice with a side salad and glass of milk, echoing standard shipboard navy meal presentation rather than the spicier or more elaborate curries found elsewhere in Japan. Some restaurants display the naval unit or ship their recipe is associated with, and a few operate inside or near the JMSDF Kure Museum and Yamato Museum area.

Because the dish is tied specifically to Kure's identity as a naval city, trying it here carries more context than eating a similar curry elsewhere, and it pairs naturally with a visit to either of the two nearby maritime museums.
access: Multiple restaurants near JR Kure Station and around the Yamato Museum and JMSDF Kure Museum area.

title: Sandankyo Gorge
summary: A 16-kilometer forested gorge northwest of Hiroshima city, designated a Special Place of Scenic Beauty, with hiking trails leading to a three-tiered waterfall deep in the valley.
description:
Sandankyo Gorge cuts through the mountains of what is now Akiota-cho, northwest of central Hiroshima, following the Shibaki River for roughly 16 kilometers, and it is officially designated a Special Place of Scenic Beauty, one of the highest such classifications in Japan and the only one held by a gorge in western Japan. The name Sandankyo, meaning roughly "three-step gorge," refers to its signature feature, Sandandaki waterfall, which drops in three distinct stages over a total height of around 130 meters.

Trail options range considerably in length: a walk as far as a spot called Kurobuchi takes roughly 50 minutes each way and covers some of the gorge's scenic highlights without requiring a full-day commitment, while reaching Sandandaki itself is a longer hike of several hours round trip through forest and along the riverbank. Small boat rides are also available on certain calmer stretches of the river within the gorge during the operating season, offering a lower-effort way to see part of the valley.

The gorge is only open seasonally, roughly from mid-April to late November, and closes over winter. Autumn is generally considered the peak season for visitors, when the forest along the trails turns to red and gold, though this also brings the largest crowds of the year.
access: About 75 to 80 minutes by express bus from Hiroshima Bus Center to Sandankyo; buses run less frequently outside peak season.
address: Togouchi, Akiota-cho, Yamagata District, Hiroshima Prefecture

title: Tomonoura
summary: A small Seto Inland Sea port town near Fukuyama said to be the only place in Japan retaining all five categories of Edo-period harbor infrastructure in something close to their original form.
description:
Tomonoura sits at the eastern edge of Hiroshima Prefecture, in the city of Fukuyama, at a point where tidal currents from either side of the Seto Inland Sea meet, which historically made it a natural waiting point for ships timing their passage with favorable tides. That role made Tomonoura an important stop for merchant ships, diplomatic missions, and travelers for centuries, and the town's layout of narrow lanes, wooden merchant houses, and sake breweries still reflects its Edo-period prosperity.

What distinguishes Tomonoura today is the survival of its full set of historic port facilities in close to original form: the stone Joyato lighthouse, tiered stone landings called gangi, a wharf, a boat repair dock, and a guardhouse station, together considered a uniquely complete surviving set of Edo-period harbor infrastructure in Japan. Walking the harbor front takes visitors past all five within a compact area.

The town's preserved streetscape and slower pace have also made it a recurring filming location for Japanese cinema and, in one well-known case, an inspiration for a Studio Ghibli film's setting, though the town's appeal predates and extends well beyond that association. A local specialty, a medicinal herbal liqueur called Homeishu, has been produced in Tomonoura for centuries and remains sold at breweries in town.
access: About 1 hour by bus from JR Fukuyama Station; Fukuyama is roughly 50 minutes to 1 hour from central Hiroshima by JR train.

title: Joyato Lighthouse
summary: A stone Edo-period beacon marking Tomonoura's harbor mouth, believed to be Japan's tallest surviving stone lighthouse from that era.
description:
Built in 1859 near the end of the Edo period, the Joyato is a solid stone tower standing at the tip of Tomonoura's harbor, historically lit at night to guide ships safely into port. It stands roughly 10 meters from its base in the water to its top, and it is generally cited as the tallest stone lighthouse surviving from the Edo period anywhere in Japan, having continued to function as a navigational aid for many decades after its construction.

The lighthouse sits at the end of a stone breakwater and jetty area that forms one of the most photographed spots in Tomonoura, with the tower, the harbor's fishing boats, and the hills across the water often composed together in a single shot, particularly around sunset. Its position at the harbor mouth also places it directly beside several of the town's other surviving Edo-period port structures, including stepped stone landings and a boat repair dock, which together make up a rare, largely intact set of historic harbor infrastructure.

Because the whole harbor area is small and walkable, the lighthouse is usually seen as part of a short loop around Tomonoura's waterfront rather than a standalone stop, and it remains a working part of the harbor rather than a purely decorative monument.
access: Within Tomonoura's harbor area, about 1 hour by bus from JR Fukuyama Station.

title: Takehara Historic Townscape
summary: A preserved Edo and Meiji-era merchant district, sometimes called 'Little Kyoto of Aki,' built on wealth from centuries of salt production and sake brewing.
description:
Takehara grew wealthy from the late 17th century onward through salt production using tidal flats along the coast, and later through sake brewing that drew on the surrounding region's rice and water, and the merchant families who profited from both industries built the substantial wooden townhouses that still line the old town's central streets today. The Honmachi district, roughly a 5-minute walk from Takehara Station, is designated as a nationally recognized Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, protecting its lattice-fronted houses, tiled roofs, and narrow lanes largely as they were in the Edo and Meiji periods.

The town is also known as the birthplace of Masataka Taketsuru, founder of Nikka Whisky and the real-life basis for a well-known NHK television drama, and the family's historic sake brewery building still stands along the main preserved street, drawing visitors interested in that connection even though it is not generally open for interior tours. Several other sake breweries in town remain active or partially open to visitors, some offering tastings.

Compared with Kyoto's more famous preserved districts, Takehara draws a fraction of the foot traffic, giving its streets a noticeably quieter, more lived-in atmosphere, with local shops, cafes, and residences still operating within the historic buildings rather than the area functioning purely as an open-air museum.
access: About 5-minute walk from JR Takehara Station; Takehara is roughly 1 hour from central Hiroshima by JR train.

title: Taketsuru Sake Brewery Street
summary: The preserved street in Takehara's old town where the sake-brewing Taketsuru family ran a business dating back to 1733, and where Masataka Taketsuru, later the founder of Nikka Whisky, grew up.
description:
The Taketsuru family operated a sake brewery in Takehara dating back to at least 1733, one of several brewing families whose wealth built the preserved merchant townscape that survives in the Honmachi district today. Masataka Taketsuru was born into this family in 1894, the third son, and grew up expected to eventually take over the family sake business before instead pursuing a very different path in alcohol production.

In 1918 Taketsuru traveled to Scotland to formally study organic chemistry and distilling, working briefly at Scottish distilleries and absorbing techniques that were, at the time, essentially unknown in Japan. He returned home, worked for other Japanese companies applying what he had learned, and eventually founded his own company in 1934, which grew into Nikka Whisky, one of Japan's two major whisky producers alongside Suntory; the story became widely known in Japan through an NHK morning drama based loosely on his life and his marriage to a Scottish wife.

The family's original brewery building still stands along Takehara's preserved main street, its exterior a recognizable stop for visitors tracing Taketsuru's story, even though the building functions today mainly as a historic landmark within the townscape rather than an operating public brewery tour.
access: Along the preserved Honmachi street, about 5-minute walk from JR Takehara Station.

title: Former Imperial Japanese Naval Academy, Etajima
summary: A guided tour through the brick campus of Japan's former naval officer academy on Etajima island, still in active use as a Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force training school.
description:
The Imperial Japanese Naval Academy was established on Etajima, an island in Hiroshima Bay, in 1888, and it trained the country's naval officers through to the end of the Second World War, including figures such as Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto and Admiral Heihachiro Togo, both covered in the on-site museum's exhibits. After the war the campus continued in a related role as the First Service School of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, which still trains personnel there today, meaning visitors are touring an active military education facility rather than a purely historic site.

The centerpiece building is a large red-brick structure completed in 1893 to a design by a British architect, built using bricks imported from England, and it remains in use for classrooms and living quarters. The grounds also include the wooden residence built in 1920 for Prince Takamatsu during his own naval service, along with the Museum of Naval History housing ship models, photographs, and personal items connected to the academy's graduates.

Visits are only possible via a guided tour, roughly 90 minutes long and led by a former JMSDF member, run on a set daily schedule with individual visitors generally not needing a reservation, though groups do. Photography inside the museum is not permitted, and admission is free; an on-site restaurant also serves navy-style curry.
access: About 20 minutes by ferry from Hiroshima Port (Ujina) to Etajima, then a short walk or bus ride to the academy; alternatively by ferry from Kure.

title: Path of Literature (Bungaku no Komichi)
summary: Twenty-four stone monuments carved with lines from writers who lived in or wrote about Onomichi, strung along the temple-hill walking course.
description:
Onomichi has produced and hosted an unusual number of Japanese writers for a small port town, among them novelist Fumiko Hayashi and Shiga Naoya, who both drew on the town's hillside views in their work. This trail collects short passages from two dozen of them, each engraved into a stone marker and placed along the same slope that connects the Cat Alley area to Senkoji Park.

Most visitors don't stop to read every stone, and that's fine — the real appeal is how the trail forces you to slow your pace on a walk you'd otherwise rush through. Between markers, the path opens onto gaps between temple roofs and citrus trees where the Onomichi Channel and the shipyards of Mukaishima appear below.

Because the trail overlaps with routes to several temples, it's easy to combine into a longer loop rather than treating it as a separate errand. Benches near a few of the stones make good rest points if the stairs elsewhere in town have worn you out, and there's rarely a crowd, since most tourists head straight for the ropeway instead.
access: Starts near Onomichi Station, about a 10-minute uphill walk; forms part of the temple walking course toward Senkoji Park.

title: Tenneiji Temple Three-Story Pagoda
summary: A weathered 14th-century pagoda that shows up in nearly every postcard shot of Onomichi's rooftops without most visitors ever learning its name.
description:
Tenneiji sits partway up the hill on the approach to Senkoji Temple, and its three-story pagoda — originally built in 1388 as a five-story structure before later rebuilding — has become the town's unofficial silhouette. It's a Nationally Designated Important Cultural Property, though the temple itself stays low-key, with no entrance fee and few staff in sight.

The pagoda's real value is as a viewpoint anchor: the gap between its roofline and the tiled houses below the hill frames the Onomichi Channel and Mukaishima's shipyard cranes in a way that photographers return to again and again, especially in the last hour before sunset when the wood tone deepens.

Because it sits directly on the standard route up to Senkoji Park and the ropeway, you'll pass it almost by accident on a temple walk rather than needing to seek it out — but it's worth pausing rather than walking straight through, since most people do exactly that.
access: About a 10-minute uphill walk from JR Onomichi Station, on the path toward Senkoji Temple and the ropeway.

title: Saikokuji Temple's Niomon Gate and Stone Steps
summary: A steep, symmetrical stone staircase framed by a red Nio guardian gate, one of the least crowded photo spots in Onomichi's temple district.
description:
Saikokuji is a working Shingon-sect temple a short walk east of the main Cat Alley cluster, and it draws far fewer visitors than the Senkoji ropeway route despite having one of the more dramatic approaches in town: a long, steep flight of stone steps rising to a vermillion Niomon gate guarded by two muscular Nio statues.

The temple grounds themselves are modest and quiet, with a small main hall and bell tower, but the staircase and gate combination is what locals point tourists toward when they want a photo without a crowd in it. Come in late afternoon when the light angles up the steps rather than flattening them.

Because Saikokuji sits slightly off the main pilgrimage route most guidebooks describe, it tends to get skipped by people on a tight schedule — which is exactly why it's worth the extra ten minutes if you've already done the busier temples nearer the station.
access: About a 15-minute walk east from JR Onomichi Station, past the main temple walking course.

title: Onomichi Cinema Museum
summary: A converted Meiji-era warehouse tracing why one small port town became a favorite filming location for directors from Ozu Yasujiro to Nobuhiko Obayashi.
description:
Onomichi's steep lanes, temple rooftops, and channel views have attracted filmmakers for nearly a century, starting with Ozu's 'Tokyo Story' in 1953 and continuing through Nobuhiko Obayashi's 'Onomichi trilogy' of teen films in the 1980s and 90s. This small museum, housed in a renovated 19th-century warehouse near the harbor, lays out that history through posters, props, and photographs rather than trying to be a general film museum.

It's a compact stop — most visitors are through in under an hour — but it gives context that changes how you see the rest of town, since several of the alleys and staircases you'll walk through later in the day are recognizable from the films on display.

Cinema Onomichi, the town's single surviving movie theater a few minutes away, still runs a program of independent and classic films in a similarly retro building funded partly by local donations, so pairing the museum with a screening (if the schedule allows) rounds out the picture of Onomichi as a genuine 'movie town' rather than just a filming backdrop.
access: About a 10-minute walk from JR Onomichi Station, near the waterfront.

affiliateLinks.label: Book an Onomichi walking or cycling tour

title: Onomichi Ramen Backstreets
summary: The small, family-run counters near Onomichi's covered arcade serving the region's signature flat noodles in a soy-and-back-fat broth.
description:
Onomichi ramen is built on a soy sauce base enriched with rendered pork or chicken back fat, which floats on top and keeps the broth hot down to the last sip — a practical trait for a town where cold sea winds cut through the streets. The flat, slightly chewy noodles are locally made rather than mass-produced, and most shops have stuck to a short menu of ramen and gyoza for decades.

The best way to experience it isn't at a single famous shop but by wandering the lanes just off the covered Onomichi shopping arcade, where several small counters, most seating fewer than ten people, have been run by the same families for two or three generations. Lines form at lunch on weekends, so an early or late visit avoids the wait.

This is a good stop to break up a day of hill-climbing between temples — cheap, fast, and filling — and it gives a much better sense of daily Onomichi life than any single sightseeing spot does.
access: Concentrated around the covered shopping arcade a few minutes' walk from JR Onomichi Station.

title: Onomichi U2
summary: A converted seaside warehouse turned cyclist-friendly complex where you can roll a loaded touring bike straight to your hotel room.
description:
Built inside a former Japan Transport Ministry maritime warehouse right on the Shimanami Kaido cycling route, Onomichi U2 was designed from the start around cyclists rather than treating them as an afterthought: rooms in its hotel section allow bikes indoors, there's an on-site rental and repair shop, and the open-plan building holds a bakery, a craft beer taproom, a restaurant, and a general store selling regional goods.

Even if you're not cycling the Shimanami Kaido, it's worth a stop for the building itself — long sightlines through raw concrete and steel trusses with the Seto Inland Sea visible through the end windows — and for a coffee or beer overlooking the water where riders set off toward Shikoku.

It sits at the actual starting point of the Shimanami Kaido route on the Onomichi side, so it works well as either a first stop before a ride or a reward stop after finishing one.
access: About a 10-minute walk from JR Onomichi Station, along the waterfront.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Shimanami Kaido cycling tour

title: Innoshima Citrus Terraces
summary: Steep hillside orchards of hassaku citrus, the tart grapefruit-like fruit that Innoshima claims as its own invention, best seen in late-winter blossom or autumn harvest.
description:
Hassaku, a citrus variety that's tart and slightly bitter compared to sweeter mandarins, was first cultivated on Innoshima in the 19th century, and the island still grows it on terraced slopes that climb steeply from the coastline. There's no single ticketed attraction here — the appeal is driving or cycling the back roads above the ferry ports, where the hillsides are laid out in these terraces and the Inland Sea appears between the rows.

The most striking time to visit is late autumn into early winter when the fruit ripens to a pale yellow-green against dark green leaves, though the terraces are quietly photogenic year-round for their sheer geometry. A few farm stands along the coastal road sell hassaku products, from raw fruit in season to marmalade and citrus sweets.

This is a spot for slow exploring rather than a checklist stop, and it rewards anyone taking the Shimanami Kaido at a relaxed pace rather than racing straight through Innoshima toward Ikuchijima.
access: Best explored by rental car or bicycle from Innoshima's ferry terminals; roughly 30–40 minutes by car from central Onomichi.

title: Setoda Sunset Beach
summary: An 800-meter stretch of sand on Ikuchijima that lives up to its name, facing due west across the Inland Sea toward the setting sun.
description:
Unlike the rocky coastlines common elsewhere on the Shimanami Kaido islands, Setoda's beach is a genuine sand strip long enough for a proper walk, with calm, shallow water that makes it popular with families in summer despite being far less crowded than mainland beaches. Facilities are simple — showers and a snack stand in season — which keeps it feeling more like a local beach than a resort.

The name isn't just marketing: the beach faces almost directly west, and on clear evenings the sun drops straight into the sea between the silhouettes of neighboring islands, a view locals rate as one of the better sunset spots along the whole cycling route.

It's an easy add-on to a Setoda visit built around Kosanji Temple or the Hirayama Ikuo Museum, and cyclists doing the Shimanami Kaido often time their day to pass through around dusk specifically for this stretch of coast.
access: About a 15-minute walk or short taxi ride from Setoda Port on Ikuchijima.

title: Shimanami Dolce Setoda
summary: A gelato shop near Kosanji Temple that turns Setoda's lemon harvest and other local ingredients into a rotating monthly menu of flavors.
description:
Setoda produces a large share of Japan's domestically grown lemons, and this gelato shop, a short walk from Kosanji Temple, is built almost entirely around using that harvest and other regional ingredients rather than importing standard flavor bases. The menu changes monthly, but citrus flavors — lemon, orange, and blends with local herbs — are a constant, alongside dairy-forward options like salted milk made with salt from nearby Hakatajima.

It's become something of an informal checkpoint for Shimanami Kaido cyclists, who stop here as a reward roughly halfway through the route, and outdoor seating faces the street so you can watch the steady stream of touring bikes pass by while you eat.

There's nothing elaborate about the shop itself — a simple counter and a short bench — but the quality of the gelato and the direct link to what's actually grown on the island make it worth seeking out over a generic convenience-store ice cream stop.
access: About a 5-minute walk from Setoda Port on Ikuchijima, near Kosanji Temple.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Shimanami Kaido cycling tour

title: Tatara Bridge Sunset Viewpoint
summary: The cable-stayed bridge marking the Hiroshima–Ehime prefectural border, best appreciated from the small park at its Ikuchijima foot rather than while riding across it.
description:
Tatara Bridge was, at the time of its 1999 completion, the longest cable-stayed bridge in the world, and it carries the Shimanami Kaido cycling path across the strait separating Ikuchijima (Hiroshima) from Omishima (Ehime). Riders cross it as a matter of course, but the more rewarding view is from Tatara Shimanami Park at its base on the Ikuchijima side, where the bridge's full cable fan is visible against the sky.

Late afternoon is the standout time to visit: the cables catch the low sun and the bridge deck silhouettes against color spreading across the Inland Sea, a combination that's made this one of the more photographed structures on the entire route.

Even non-cyclists can reach the viewpoint by car, making it one of the few Shimanami Kaido highlights that doesn't require getting on a bike, though riding across the bridge itself — a gentle, well-protected climb — is a highlight for anyone doing the route.
access: At Tatara Shimanami Park on Ikuchijima, roughly 50 minutes by car from central Onomichi via the Shimanami Kaido expressway.

title: Mukaishima Shipyard Skyline and Backstreets
summary: The working shipbuilding island facing Onomichi across a channel barely 200 meters wide, where cranes light up in shifting colors after dark.
description:
Mukaishima sits directly across the narrow Onomichi Channel from the mainland, close enough that a small ferry crossing takes only a few minutes, and its skyline of shipyard cranes has become part of Onomichi's own visual identity — visible in the background of countless photos taken from the hillside temples on the other side. Rather than viewing it only from Onomichi, crossing over lets you walk the residential backstreets that run alongside the working docks, where the scale of the ships under construction is much more apparent up close.

At night, several of the crane structures are lit in slowly changing colors, a low-key light display that's easy to miss unless you know to look for it, best seen either from the Mukaishima side itself or from the Onomichi waterfront after dark.

This isn't a polished sightseeing route — it's a genuine industrial neighborhood — but that's exactly its appeal for visitors who've already covered Onomichi's temple hill and want a sense of the town's other economic backbone.
access: Passenger ferries cross from Onomichi's waterfront to Mukaishima in about 3–5 minutes; bridges also connect the island for cars and bicycles.

affiliateLinks.label: Book an Onomichi walking or cycling tour

title: Hishio Beach
summary: A small, low-key swimming beach on Mukaishima that stays mostly local, a short hop from Onomichi's tourist crowds.
description:
Hishio Beach and its neighbor Tachibana Coast are where Onomichi and Mukaishima families actually go swimming in summer, rather than a curated tourist beach — expect basic changing facilities, calm shallow water suited to children, and a noticeably local crowd compared to the temple hill on the other side of the channel.

The setting is unglamorous but pleasant: modest hills behind the beach, small fishing boats moored nearby, and views back across the water toward the shipyards and Onomichi's hillside. It's not a destination in itself worth crossing the country for, but for visitors staying in Onomichi for more than a day, it's an easy way to cool off away from the crowds around the ropeway and Cat Alley.

Combine it with a walk through Mukaishima's shipyard backstreets or a simple bicycle loop of the island, since the beach alone is a fairly quick stop.
access: About a 10–15 minute bicycle or bus ride from the Mukaishima ferry landing.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Shimanami Kaido cycling tour

title: Mount Misen Daisho-in Trail
summary: A roughly two-hour hike up Miyajima's sacred mountain along a moss-covered stone staircase through old-growth forest, for visitors willing to skip the ropeway.
description:
Mount Misen, at 535 meters, has been considered sacred since long before Itsukushima Shrine was built, and it's possible to reach the summit either by ropeway or on foot via three marked trails. The Daisho-in course, starting at the temple of the same name, is generally rated the most scenic and slightly less steep than the alternatives, climbing through a nearly unbroken stone staircase shaded by the Misen Primeval Forest, a nationally protected natural monument.

The hike takes most people around ninety minutes to two hours one way, and unlike the ropeway crowd, hikers tend to have long stretches of the trail to themselves, with only birdsong and the occasional wild monkey for company (feeding them is prohibited).

At the summit, the view stretches across the Seto Inland Sea back toward Hiroshima city on clear days, and hikers can either walk back down or take the ropeway down instead, which is a reasonable compromise for tired legs after an honestly earned view.
access: Trailhead at Daisho-in Temple, about a 20-minute walk from Miyajima Pier; allow roughly 1.5–2 hours to the summit.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Miyajima Island day tour

title: Omotesando Oyster Stalls
summary: The grilled-oyster counters lining Miyajima's main approach street, where you can watch the whole process from open flame to shell before eating.
description:
Hiroshima Bay produces roughly half of Japan's farmed oysters, and Miyajima's 350-meter Omotesando arcade, running from the ferry pier toward Itsukushima Shrine, is where much of that harvest gets grilled on the spot. Several small shops and street stalls along the street shuck and grill oysters over open charcoal right in front of customers, served simply with a squeeze of citrus or in variations like garlic butter and cheese.

Beyond the classic grilled oyster, the arcade has also produced odder hybrids that locals treat with a mix of pride and amusement, including deep-fried oyster curry bread sold at a bakery a few doors down — a genuinely Miyajima-specific snack rather than a generic tourist treat.

Eating your way down Omotesando works well as a pre- or post-shrine activity, since the street sits directly between the ferry pier and Itsukushima Shrine's entrance; just budget extra time, since the smell of grilling oysters makes it hard to walk past without stopping at least once.
access: Directly ahead from Miyajima Pier, forming the main approach street to Itsukushima Shrine.

title: Kure Navy Curry Restaurants
summary: The dish Kure claims as its culinary trademark: mild, roux-thickened curry served the way the old Imperial Navy and today's Self-Defense Force prepare it.
description:
The Imperial Japanese Navy adopted curry rice from the British Royal Navy in the late 19th century as an easy way to feed large crews a balanced meal, and Friday became unofficial 'curry day' to help sailors, who had no weekends at sea, keep track of the days. Kure, as one of Japan's principal naval bases, leaned into this history, and today dozens of restaurants across the city serve curry based on recipes tied to specific ships or eras, each registered and stamped as an official 'Kure Navy Curry' by a local certification project.

Compared to typical Japanese household curry, navy curry tends to be milder and more vegetable-forward, closer to the original British-influenced recipe, often served with a side of milk, a tradition tied to the navy's efforts to prevent beriberi among sailors.

Restaurants around JR Kure Station and near the Yamato Museum post the certification mark clearly, so you can spot an 'official' bowl versus a generic curry shop — a fun scavenger-hunt element if you're visiting the museums nearby.
access: Restaurants are concentrated near JR Kure Station and around the Yamato Museum waterfront district.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Kure day trip from Hiroshima

title: Rengadori Shopping Arcade
summary: Kure's 420-meter covered shopping street, notable as the site of Japan's first retractable arcade roof, still run mostly by independent local shops.
description:
Rengadori (literally 'brick street,' also known as Kure Nakadori) runs through the center of Kure and became something of a small landmark in retail architecture when it installed Japan's first retractable roof arcade in 1990, allowing the covering to open on clear days rather than staying permanently enclosed like a typical shotengai.

The arcade itself is a mix of clothing shops, bakeries, cafes, and casual restaurants, several of which serve the city's certified navy curry, along with older stores that have operated there for decades. It's a working commercial street for Kure residents rather than a tourist attraction, which is exactly why it's a useful stop — it shows a side of the city the naval museums don't.

Because it's close to JR Kure Station and sits on the way toward the Yamato Museum waterfront, it's easy to fold into a museum day without a special detour, and it's a reliable place to grab a casual lunch between exhibits.
access: About a 5-minute walk from JR Kure Station.

title: Fujii Shuzo Sake Brewery
summary: A family sake brewery operating from the same alley in Takehara's historic district for around 150 years, with tastings poured a few steps from the brewing tanks.
description:
Tucked into one of the narrower side alleys of Takehara's preserved merchant district, Fujii Shuzo has been brewing sake since 1863, making it one of the few producers still operating from within the historic townscape rather than a modern facility outside it. The brewery won a top prize at Japan's first national sake competition in 1907 and continues to use rice grown locally along with mountain spring water for its junmai-shu.

Visitors can taste a rotating selection of the brewery's sake on-site, and an attached soba restaurant makes it possible to turn a quick tasting stop into a proper light meal, pairing the sake with simple noodle dishes rather than rushing straight back out to the street.

Because it sits inside the historic district itself, a visit here doubles as a way to see the interior of one of the old merchant buildings up close, with worn wooden beams and brewing equipment that make the connection between Takehara's Edo-era wealth and its sake tradition much more concrete than reading about it.
access: Within Takehara's historic townscape district, about a 10-minute walk from JR Takehara Station.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Takehara sake tasting tour

title: Taichoro Guesthouse Viewpoint
summary: A 1690s reception hall built to host Korean diplomatic missions, whose tatami room frames Benten-jima and Sensui-jima islands like a living painting.
description:
Taichoro was built in 1690 as part of Fukuzenji Temple specifically to receive Korean embassy delegations traveling to Edo, and the hall's main tatami room is positioned so that its window opening frames the view of Benten-jima and Sensui-jima islands in the bay almost like a hung scroll painting — a design choice contemporary visitors still comment on today. One of the Korean envoys reportedly described the view as the most beautiful in Japan east of Korea, a line still quoted locally.

The hall itself is simple and uncrowded, a rare chance to sit in a genuine Edo-period diplomatic reception space rather than viewing one from behind a rope barrier, and the low admission fee keeps it from feeling like a major tourist draw despite the significance of the site.

It's a short uphill walk from Tomonoura's main harbor streets, making it easy to combine with a walk through the port town itself, and the elevated position gives a different, calmer vantage point over the bay than the harborside views below.
access: About a 10-minute walk uphill from Tomonoura's central bus stop.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Tomonoura day trip from Hiroshima

title: Iroha Maru Museum
summary: A small warehouse museum built around the 1867 wreck of a steamship owned by Sakamoto Ryoma's trading company, sunk just off Tomonoura's coast.
description:
In 1867, the Iroha Maru, a steamship operated by the trading and paramilitary company of samurai reformer Sakamoto Ryoma, collided with a much larger vessel from the Kishu domain near Tomonoura and sank, triggering a tense negotiation over compensation that became one of the more dramatic episodes in the years leading up to the Meiji Restoration. Ryoma himself came to Tomonoura to negotiate the settlement, staying in the port town during the dispute.

This small museum, set inside an atmospheric old warehouse near the harbor, displays artifacts recovered from underwater surveys of the wreck alongside documents and models explaining the incident and its political stakes.

It's a minor footnote in most general histories of the Meiji Restoration but a significant local story in Tomonoura, and the museum's compact, unpolished setting — creaky floors, dim lighting, genuine salvaged objects — gives it more atmosphere than its small size would suggest. Easy to fit in alongside the port town walk and Taichoro.
access: Within Tomonoura's harbor district, about a 5-minute walk from the central bus stop.

title: Saijo Sake Brewery Street
summary: Seven working sake breweries with tall brick chimneys lined up within walking distance of Saijo Station, one of Japan's three historically recognized sake capitals.
description:
Saijo, part of Higashihiroshima City, ranks alongside Nada in Hyogo and Fushimi in Kyoto as one of Japan's three traditionally recognized centers of sake production, a status built on the area's naturally soft, mineral-balanced groundwater, ideal for brewing. Seven breweries, some with buildings and brick chimneys dating to the 1800s, line a single street running from just outside JR Saijo Station, close enough together to visit several in one afternoon on foot.

Most breweries operate small retail shops selling bottles unavailable outside the region, and several offer tastings or brief tours explaining their specific brewing style, letting visitors compare noticeably different sake within a short walk rather than relying on descriptions alone.

The street was recognized in 2017 as one of Japan's top heritage sites of the 20th century, and unlike more famous sake regions, it remains easy to visit as a half-day trip directly from Hiroshima city by train, without needing a car or an organized tour.
access: About a 5-minute walk from JR Saijo Station; roughly 30–40 minutes from Hiroshima Station by JR train.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Saijo sake tasting tour

title: Kamotsuru Sake Brewery
summary: The Saijo brewery whose daiginjo was poured at a 2014 dinner for a sitting U.S. president, still selling tastings a short walk from the station.
description:
Kamotsuru has been one of the defining names on Saijo's brewery street since the Edo period, when feudal lords stopping in the town favored its sake, and it later became a pioneer of daiginjo — sake milled down to a small fraction of the original rice grain for an exceptionally refined flavor — with its Tokusei Gold label released in 1958. The brewery's profile jumped internationally in 2014 when its sake was served at a state dinner between then-President Barack Obama and Prime Minister Shinzo Abe.

The brewery's shop and tasting counter sit within the historic brick-and-timber building on Saijo's brewery street, and visitors can sample a range from everyday table sake up to premium daiginjo, with staff generally willing to explain the differences in production and taste rather than just pouring and moving on.

It's one stop among several on the same street, so most visitors treat it as an anchor point for a broader brewery walk rather than a single destination, but its history and international profile make it a reasonable starting point if you only have time for one.
access: On Saijo Sake Brewery Street, about a 5-minute walk from JR Saijo Station.
