title: Shinshoji Zen Museum and Gardens
summary: A working Zen temple in the hills above Fukuyama that mixes a relocated 17th-century hall, a teahouse in the style of Sen no Rikyu, and contemporary art in one sprawling complex.
description:
Shinshoji is a Rinzai Zen temple founded in 1965, but rather than presenting as a single historic structure, its roughly 230,000-square-meter grounds function more like a curated cultural park: a 17th-century temple hall relocated whole from Shiga Prefecture, a reconstructed teahouse based on the design principles of tea master Sen no Rikyu, and a temple administration building designed by architect Terunobu Fujimori around a red-pine theme, sitting alongside spaces for contemporary art exhibitions.

Visitors can join Zen meditation sessions or try sutra copying (shakyo), options that make this one of the more accessible places in the region to experience Buddhist practice directly rather than only viewing a temple from outside.

The mix of eras and disciplines — Edo-period architecture, modern design, contemporary art — makes Shinshoji unusual among temple visits in Hiroshima Prefecture, and its hillside setting outside central Fukuyama keeps it well clear of the crowds around the city's more famous castle.
access: About a 15-minute taxi ride from JR Fukuyama Station; roughly 1 hour from Hiroshima Station via Fukuyama.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Fukuyama day trip from Hiroshima

title: Mihara Castle Ruins
summary: A 16th-century 'floating castle' whose remaining stone foundations sit directly beneath the platforms of JR Mihara Station, visible from a moving train.
description:
Mihara Castle was built in the mid-16th century by warlord Kobayakawa Takakage on a small tidal islet, engineered so that at high tide the walls appeared to rise straight out of the sea — earning it a reputation as one of Japan's earliest 'floating castles.' Much of the original site was built over as the city and its rail line developed, and JR Mihara Station now sits almost directly atop the former castle grounds.

What survives — stone foundations, a section of moat, and the reconstructed Funairi turret — is accessible on a short walk from the station, and part of the old stonework is visible from the train platforms themselves, an odd but memorable detail for a castle site.

Mihara doesn't draw the crowds of Hiroshima's better-known castle towns, which makes this a low-key stop for anyone changing trains through the city on the way to or from Onomichi or Shikoku, worth ten minutes rather than a special trip.
access: Directly adjacent to JR Mihara Station; roughly 40–50 minutes from Hiroshima Station by JR train.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Mihara or Onomichi day trip

title: Mihara Octopus Cuisine
summary: A city that has fully embraced its identity as one of the Seto Inland Sea's leading octopus grounds, decorating its train station and menus accordingly.
description:
Mihara's stretch of the Inland Sea produces octopus known locally for its firm, dense texture, a result of the strong tidal currents that pass through the strait, and the city has made the animal into something close to a civic mascot: octopus statues and decorative flags appear around JR Mihara Station, and restaurants across town build menus specifically around it.

Preparations range from simple boiled octopus served with vinegar-miso sauce to grilled skewers, octopus tempura, and rice dishes mixed with diced octopus, giving visitors a chance to compare textures and flavors across several dishes in one meal rather than trying just one style.

Because Mihara is a common transfer point for travelers moving between Hiroshima city, Onomichi, and Shikoku, it's an easy place to build in a meal stop, and the octopus theme gives it a distinct identity that's easy to overlook if you only think of the city as a train junction.
access: Restaurants concentrated around JR Mihara Station; roughly 40–50 minutes from Hiroshima Station by JR train.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Mihara or Onomichi day trip

title: Miyoshi Mononoke Museum
summary: A museum dedicated to yokai folklore, built around one collector's lifetime archive and Miyoshi's own starring role in a centuries-old monster legend.
description:
Formally the Yumoto Koichi Memorial Japan Yokai Museum, this collection opened in 2019 around the lifelong archive of Yumoto Koichi, a leading scholar of yokai — the ghosts, monsters, and spirits of Japanese folklore. The holdings run to more than 5,000 objects, spanning Edo-period woodblock prints, including Toriyama Sekien's influential 18th-century bestiary of supernatural creatures, through to modern illustrated and sculptural interpretations.

Miyoshi was chosen as the museum's home specifically because of its own local legend, the Inou Mononoke Roku, an Edo-period account of a young samurai's month-long haunting by a parade of yokai, which has been retold in scrolls, picture books, and manga for centuries and is treated in the museum as a foundational regional ghost story.

The museum sits well off the main Hiroshima tourist circuit in the inland city of Miyoshi, making it a deliberate detour rather than a casual add-on, but for anyone interested in Japanese folklore or the visual history behind modern yokai-influenced pop culture, it's a far deeper collection than the small city's size would suggest.
access: About a 15-minute bus ride from JR Miyoshi Station; roughly 1.5 hours from Hiroshima Station by JR train or highway bus.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Miyoshi day trip from Hiroshima

title: Taishakukyo Gorge
summary: An 18-kilometer limestone gorge in Hiroshima's mountainous north, where a boat ride under a natural stone arch replaces the usual hiking-trail approach to gorge scenery.
description:
Carved by the Taishaku River through limestone terrain in Shobara, Taishakukyo stretches roughly 18 kilometers and is often described as one of the largest limestone gorges in Japan, with sheer rock walls, caves, and a large natural stone bridge, Onbashi, formed by the collapse of an underground cavern roof.

Unlike most Japanese gorges that are experienced primarily on foot, a central stretch of Taishakukyo is explored by small sightseeing boat across Shinryuko lake, giving a low-effort way to take in the cliff faces and forest color, particularly striking during autumn foliage from late October into November.

Because it sits well north of Hiroshima city in a sparsely populated part of the prefecture, Taishakukyo requires a car or a fairly involved bus connection to reach, which keeps visitor numbers modest even in peak foliage season compared to more accessible nature spots — a genuine advantage for anyone trying to avoid crowds while still seeing dramatic scenery.
access: Best reached by car, roughly 1.5–2 hours from Hiroshima city; limited bus connections run from JR Shobara or Tojo stations.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Hiroshima nature and gorge tour

title: Etajima Museum of Naval History
summary: A brick former Imperial Naval Academy campus, still an active Self-Defense Force officer school, open to the public through guided tours only.
description:
The Imperial Japanese Navy moved its officer academy from Tokyo to Etajima Island in 1888, and the resulting campus — including an 1893 Officer Candidate School and a grand 1917 Ceremonial Hall, both built with brick imported from Britain, the nation that helped modernize Japan's navy — trained generations of officers through the Second World War. The campus now operates as the JMSDF's First Service School, an active officer training institution, and the historic buildings remain in daily use rather than being preserved as a static museum piece.

Public access is limited to guided tours, run several times daily and more frequently on weekends, which take visitors through the parade grounds, the ceremonial hall's ornate interior, and an Education Reference Museum holding roughly 16,000 naval artifacts, of which about a thousand are on rotating display.

Because it's a working military school rather than a heritage site catering to tourists, the visit has a distinctly formal, unpolished character — no gift shop sheen, just genuine institutional history — reached by a short ferry hop from Kure that most Hiroshima visitors never think to take.
access: About a 10-minute ferry ride from Kure port; guided tours run on a fixed daily schedule, more frequent on weekends.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Kure and Etajima day trip

title: Etajima Coastal Cycling Route
summary: A quiet island loop of citrus groves and fishing coves a short ferry hop from Kure, popular with local cyclists but almost unknown to overseas visitors.
description:
Etajima is best known internationally, if at all, for its former Imperial Naval Academy, but the rest of the island — connected to the mainland by bridge as well as ferry — is a mix of small fishing settlements, hillside citrus orchards, and quiet coastal roads that make it a favorite low-traffic cycling loop for residents of Kure and Hiroshima city.

Bicycle rental is available near the main ferry terminals, and a loop of the island's coastal roads takes most riders three to five hours depending on stops, passing beaches, small Shinto shrines tucked into the hillside, and roadside stands selling citrus in season.

Compared to the internationally famous Shimanami Kaido, Etajima's routes are shorter, flatter in stretches, and see a fraction of the cyclist traffic, making it a good option for a more relaxed half-day ride, or for visitors basing themselves in Kure who want an outdoor activity beyond the naval museums.
access: Ferries to Etajima run from Kure port (about 10 minutes) and from Hiroshima Port (Ujina); bicycle rental available near the terminals.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Kure and Etajima day trip

title: Mitarai Historic Port Town
summary: A once-thriving Edo-period pleasure port on a remote island at the end of the Tobishima Kaido, its narrow lanes barely touched since shipping routes moved elsewhere.
description:
Mitarai, on Osakikamijima at the far end of the Tobishima Kaido island chain southeast of Kure, grew wealthy in the Edo period as a waiting harbor where ships timed their passage through the Inland Sea's currents, developing a lively pleasure district of teahouses and merchant houses to serve sailors passing through. When steamship routes and modern shipping bypassed the island in the 20th century, the town's growth essentially stopped, leaving its Edo and Meiji-era streetscape unusually intact and now protected as a national Important Preservation District.

Walking the narrow lanes today, past latticed wooden facades, a preserved public bathhouse, and a small red bridge over the old canal, there's little sense of having to imagine the historic scene — it's simply still there, largely because nothing came along to replace it.

Mitarai sees very few tourists even by the standards of Hiroshima Prefecture's back roads, since reaching it means driving or busing the full length of the Tobishima Kaido chain, but for visitors willing to make the trip, it's about as close as the region gets to an untouched Edo-period port town.
access: About a 1.5–2 hour drive from Kure via the Tobishima Kaido island road, or infrequent bus service from Kure Station; can also be reached by ferry.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Kure and Tobishima Kaido day trip

title: Tobishima Kaido Scenic Drive
summary: A quieter, less-touristed cousin of the Shimanami Kaido, stringing together seven small islands south of Kure with a chain of low bridges over turquoise water.
description:
While the Shimanami Kaido gets most of the international attention, the Tobishima Kaido, connecting seven islands south of Kure — including Kurahashijima, Nuwajima, Kamikamagarijima, and Osakikamijima — offers a similar experience of island-hopping over water on a much smaller, quieter scale, with far less traffic and almost no organized tour groups.

The road is popular with local cyclists and drivers for its clear water, small citrus-farming communities, and short bridges that rarely involve the long climbs of the Shimanami Kaido's larger crossings, making it a more relaxed ride for cyclists who want scenery without the crowds or the distance.

The route culminates at Mitarai, the historic port town on Osakikamijima, giving the drive or ride a genuine destination rather than just a loop back to the mainland, and the whole stretch can be done as a day trip by car from Kure or as a longer, more leisurely cycling route for those with more time.
access: Starts near Kure and runs south via a chain of bridges; best done by car or bicycle, roughly 1.5–2 hours end to end by car.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Tobishima Kaido cycling or driving tour

title: Hijiyama Park and Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art
summary: A free hilltop park that quietly rivals Peace Memorial Park for cherry blossoms, home to Japan's first public museum built specifically for contemporary art.
description:
Hijiyama Park, opened in 1903 as Hiroshima's first city park, sits on a modest 71-meter hill in Minami-ku with clear views across the urban grid toward the bay, and its roughly 1,300 cherry trees make it one of the city's major hanami spots each spring — busy with local families and office parties, but noticeably less crowded than Peace Memorial Park during the same season.

At the top of the hill, the Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art, designed by metabolist architect Kisho Kurokawa and opened in 1989, holds the distinction of being the first Japanese public museum built entirely around contemporary art rather than adding a contemporary wing to an existing collection. Its permanent holdings run to more than 1,400 works addressing art movements since 1945, several engaging directly with Hiroshima's own postwar history.

The park itself has no gate or entrance fee and no closing time, making it a flexible stop whether you're there for a quick walk, a full cherry-blossom picnic, or a dedicated museum visit — a useful counterweight to Hiroshima's downtown sights for visitors who want green space without leaving the city center.
access: About a 15-minute walk from Hiroshima Station, or a short ride on the Hiroden streetcar to Hijiyama-shita stop.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Hiroshima city walking tour

title: Nagarekawa Nightlife District
summary: Hiroshima's densest concentration of bars, izakaya, and karaoke boxes packed into a compact grid of alleys just east of the main Hondori shopping street.
description:
Nagarekawa is Hiroshima's largest entertainment district, a dense grid of narrow streets holding well over a thousand bars, izakaya, snack bars, and karaoke spots within a few walking-distance blocks east of the central Hondori and Parco shopping area. It began as a haunt for local artists and writers before shifting decades ago into the city's primary nightlife zone, and today it draws everyone from salarymen on after-work drinks to visitors chasing a late-night bowl of Hiroshima-style tsukemen.

Unlike a single curated food street, Nagarekawa rewards wandering — small standing bars seating six people sit beside multi-floor karaoke complexes and casual yakitori counters, and the mix changes block by block. Prices skew reasonable compared to similar districts in Osaka or Tokyo, and English menus are less common here, which keeps the area feeling distinctly local rather than tourist-oriented.

It gets going after dark and stays lively well past midnight on weekends, making it a natural evening counterpart to a daytime spent at the Peace Park or Hiroshima Castle a short walk away.
access: About a 10-minute walk from Hiroden Kamiyacho-nishi or Kamiyacho-higashi streetcar stops, just east of Hondori.

affiliateLinks.label: Book a Hiroshima food and nightlife tour

title: Ninoshima Island
summary: A half-hour ferry ride from Hiroshima Port, this quiet island mixes a sandy sunset beach with the somber remains of a wartime quarantine and casualty station.
description:
Ninoshima sits close enough to Hiroshima Port that it functions as a genuine local getaway rather than a tourist destination, with a laid-back beach where residents come to swim and watch the sunset over the Inland Sea, well away from the crowds of Miyajima.

The island's more difficult history sits alongside that leisure use: from 1895 it operated as a military quarantine station for the Imperial Army and Navy, and in August 1945, after the bombing of Hiroshima, it became one of the sites where thousands of injured and dying victims were brought for treatment, many of whom did not survive. Ruins of the old quarantine facilities, including an ammunition depot and lookout post, remain on the island, and a memorial marks the mass burial site of bombing victims.

Most visitors come either for the beach and a quiet walk in the hills, or specifically to see the historical remains, and few combine both in one short visit — but either way, Ninoshima offers a side of Hiroshima's story, and a version of its coastline, that the busier tourist circuit doesn't show.
access: About a 25–30 minute ferry ride from Hiroshima Port (Ujina), reachable from central Hiroshima by streetcar and ferry.

title: Kanawa Island Oyster Rafts
summary: A small, low-profile island near Kure built almost entirely around oyster farming, where visitors can eat straight off the rafts at simple dockside restaurants.
description:
While Miyajima gets the tourist attention for Hiroshima's oyster culture, much of the actual farming happens on the calmer, more sheltered waters around smaller islands like Kanawajima, near Kure, where rows of floating rafts suspend oyster ropes just offshore. The island itself is modest and residential, with no major sightseeing beyond the working waterfront, but a handful of simple restaurants and direct-sale outlets serve oysters harvested essentially that morning.

Season runs roughly from autumn through spring, when the water is coolest, and prices tend to run noticeably lower than at more touristed spots, since there's little markup built in for foot traffic that mostly isn't there. Some operators also run short boat trips out to the rafts themselves for visitors who want to see the farming process rather than just eat the result.

It's a spot aimed at people who already know they like oysters and want to see where a large share of Japan's supply actually comes from, rather than a general sightseeing stop — best combined with a Kure museum day, given the short distance between them.
access: A short ferry or car ride from central Kure; check current oyster restaurant operating days before visiting, as many run seasonally.
